nodes.name: Subset notation $\subset$
nodes.statement: In this paper, we use $\subset$ for the subset relation includes equality, namely, $A\subset B$ means $x\in A\Rightarrow x\in B$ holds for all $x$.

nodes.name: Type-based many-sorted algebra, term and variety
nodes.statement: Let $S$ be a cardinal. \begin{enumerate} \item An $S$-sorted type is a tuple $(F,\mathrm{ar},{\rm dom},{\rm cod})$ that satisfies the following conditions: \begin{itemize} \item $F$ is a set. \item $\mathrm{ar}:F\rightarrow {\rm Card}$, where ${\rm Card}$ is the class of all cardinals. \item ${\rm dom},{\rm cod}$ are functions defined on $F$ and satisfy ${\rm dom}(f):\mathrm{ar}(f)\rightarrow S$, ${\rm cod}(f)\in S$ for each $f\in F$. \end{itemize} \item For an $S$-sorted type $F$, $F$-algebra is a pair $(A,\tau)$ that satisfies the following conditions: \begin{itemize} \item $A=(A_s)_{s\in S}$ is an $S$-indexed family of sets. \item $\tau$ is a function defined on $F$ and $\tau(f)$ is a mapping $\prod_{i\in\mathrm{ar}(f)}A_{{\rm dom}(f)(i)}\rightarrow A_{{\rm cod}(f)}$ for each $f\in F$. \end{itemize} \item For an infinite cardinal $\kappa$, $F$ is said $<\mathclose\kappa$-ary if $\mathrm{ar}(f)<\kappa$ hold for all $f\in F$. \item The height of $F$ is defined as \[ \mathrm{Ht}(F):= \begin{cases} \omega_0& \text{if }F\text{ is finitary},\\ \min\{\kappa\in\mathrm{Ord}\mid {\rm cf}(\kappa) >\mathrm{ar}(f)\text{ for all }f\in F\}& \text{ if }F\text{ is infinitary}, \end{cases} \] where $\omega_0$ is the minimum infinite ordinal, $\mathrm{Ord}$ is the class of all ordinals, and ${\rm cf}(\kappa)$ is the cofinality of $\kappa$, i.e., the minimum cardinal $\alpha$ such that there exists an $\alpha$-indexed family $(\lambda_i)_{i\in\alpha}$ of cardinals that satisfies $\lambda_i<\kappa$ (for all $i\in\alpha$) and $\sup_{i\in\alpha} \lambda_i=\kappa$. \item For an $S$-sorted type $F$, an ordinal $\alpha$, a cardinal $\lambda$, a mapping $v:\lambda\rightarrow S$ and an element $s\in S$, the set $T_{\alpha,(\lambda,v,s)}$ of all $(\lambda,v)$-ary $s$-valued terms of $F$ with complexity less than $\alpha$ is inductively defined as follows: \begin{itemize} \item $T_{0,(\lambda,v,s)}:=\{x_i\mid v(i)=s,i\in\lambda\}$. (The set of variable symbols.) \item $T_{\alpha+1,(\lambda,v,s)}:=T_{\alpha,(\lambda,v,s)}\cup \{(f,(t_i)_{i\in \mathrm{ar}(F)})\mid f\in F,t_i\in T_{\alpha,(\lambda,v,{\rm dom}(f)(i))},{\rm cod}(f)=s\}$. \item $T_{\alpha,(\lambda,v,s)}:=\bigcup_{\beta<\alpha} T_{\beta,(\lambda,v,s)}$ if $\alpha$ is a limit ordinal. \end{itemize} The set of all $(\lambda,v)$-ary $s$-valued terms of $F$ is $T_{\mathrm{Ht}(F),(\lambda,v,s)}$. \item The action of terms to an algebra $(A,\tau)$ is inductively defined as follows: \begin{itemize} \item For $x_i\in T_{0,(\lambda,v,v(i))}$, $\tau(x_i):\prod_{j\in \lambda}A_{v(j)}\rightarrow A_{v(i)}$ is defined as $(a_j)_{j\in\lambda}\mapsto a_i$. \item If $t=(f,(t_i)_{i\in \mathrm{ar}(F)})$, $\tau(t):\prod_{j\in \lambda}A_{v(j)}\rightarrow A_{{\rm cod}(f)}$ is defined as \[ (a_j)_{j\in\lambda}\mapsto \tau(f)(\tau(t_i)(a_j)_{j\in\lambda})_{i\in\mathrm{ar}(F)}. \] \end{itemize} \item For $s\in S$, An $s$-sorted identity is a pair of two $s$-valued terms. The tuple $(t_1,t_2)$ is usually denoted by $t_1=t_2$ when it is considered as an identity. A relation $(A,\tau) \models t_1=t_2$ between an algebra $(A,\tau)$ and an equation $t_1=t_2$ is defined by $\tau(t_1)=\tau(t_2)$. \item An equational theory is a set of identities. An algebra $A$ and an equational theory $E$, $A\models E$ means $A\models e$ for all $e\in E$. A pair $(F,E)$ of type $F$ and equational theory $E$ is called a type with equational theory. \item A class $\mathcal{V}$ of $F$-algebras is said a variety if there exists an equational theory $E$ such that \mbox{$\mathcal{V}=\{A\mid A\models E\}$}. The variety of $F$-algebras defined by $E$ is denoted by $\mathcal{V}_{(F,E)}$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Classical definitions of $S$-sorted types, $F$-algebras, height, terms and their action, identities, equational theories and varieties $\mathcal{V}_{(F,E)}$.

nodes.name: $S$-sorted $<\kappa$-ary clone
nodes.statement: Let $S$ and $\kappa$ be cardinals. An $S$-sorted $<\mathclose\kappa$-ary clone $M$ is a many-sorted algebra satisfying the following conditions: \begin{itemize} \item (Sort) The set of all sorts of $M$ consists of tuples $(\lambda,v,s)$, where $\lambda<\kappa$ is a cardinal, $v:\lambda\rightarrow S$ and $s\in S$. \item (Operation) $M$ has the following two types of operations: \begin{itemize} \item (Projection) For $\lambda<\kappa$, $v:\lambda\rightarrow S$ and $i\in \lambda$, $M$ has a nullary operation $\pi_{(\lambda,v,i)}\in M_{(\lambda,v,v(i))}$. \item (Composition) For $\lambda_k<\kappa, v_k:\lambda_k\rightarrow S$ ($k=1,2$) and $s\in S$, $M$ has an operation \[ c_{(\lambda_1,v_1,s),(\lambda_2,v_2)}: M_{(\lambda_1,v_1,s)}\times \prod_{i\in\lambda_1}M_{(\lambda_2,v_2,v_1(i))} \rightarrow M_{(\lambda_2,v_2,s)} \] \end{itemize} \item (Axiom) $M$ satisfying the following equations: \begin{itemize} \item (Associativity) For $\lambda_k<\kappa,v_k:\lambda_k\rightarrow S$ ($k=1,2,3$) and $s\in S$, \begin{align*} &c_{(\lambda_1,v_1,s),(\lambda_3,v_3)}(x, (c_{(\lambda_2,v_2,v_1(i)),(\lambda_3,v_3)}(y_i,(z_{j})_{j\in\lambda_2}))_{i\in\lambda_1})\\ =& c_{(\lambda_2,v_2,s),(\lambda_3,v_3)} (c_{(\lambda_1,v_1,s),(\lambda_2,v_2)}(x,(y_i)_{i\in\lambda_1}), (z_j)_{j\in\lambda_2}). \end{align*} \item (Outer identity law) For $\lambda_k<\kappa,v_k:\lambda_k\rightarrow S$ ($k=1,2$) and $i_0\in\lambda_1$ \[ c_{(\lambda_1,v_1,v_1(i_0)),(\lambda_2,v_2)} (\pi_{(\lambda_1,v_1,i_0)},(x_i)_{i\in\lambda_1}) =x_{i_0}. \] \item (Inner identity law) For $\lambda<\kappa,v:\lambda\rightarrow S$ and $s\in S$, \[ c_{(\lambda,v,s),(\lambda,v)}(x,(\pi_{(\lambda,v,i)})_{i\in\lambda}) =x. \] \end{itemize} \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: A many-sorted clone: sorts $(\lambda,v,s)$, projections and composition operations satisfying associativity and outer/inner identity laws.

nodes.name: $M$-algebra and the category $\mathrm{Cat}(\mathcal{V}(M))$
nodes.statement: Let $S$ and $\kappa$ be a cardinals, $M$ be an $S$-sorted $<\mathclose\kappa$-ary clone. A tuple $(A,\tau)$ is said an $M$-algebra if the following conditions hold: \begin{itemize} \item $A=(A_s)_{s\in S}$ is an $S$-indexed family of sets. \item $\tau=(\tau_{(\lambda,v,s)})$ is a family of mappings, where $(\lambda,v,s)$ runs all tuples that satisfy $\lambda<\kappa$, $v:\lambda \rightarrow S$ and $s\in S$, and $\tau_{(\lambda,v,s)}$ is defined on $M_{(\lambda,v,s)}$ and $\tau_{(\lambda,v,s)}(f)$ is a mapping $\prod_{i\in\lambda}A_{v(i)}\rightarrow A_s$ for each $f\in M_{(\lambda,v,s)}$. \item For $f\in M_{(\lambda_1,v_1,s)}$, $(g_i)_{i\in\lambda_1}\in \prod_{i\in\lambda_1}M_{(\lambda_2,v_2,v_1(i))}$ and $(a_j)_{j\in\lambda_2}\in\prod_{j\in\lambda_2}A_{v_2(j)}$, the following equation holds: \[ \tau_{(\lambda_2,v_2,s)}(c_{(\lambda_1,v_1,s),(\lambda_2,v_2)}(f,(g_i)_{i\in\lambda_1}))(a_{j})_{j\in\lambda_2} =\tau_{(\lambda_1,v_1,s)}(f)(\tau_{(\lambda_2,v_2,v_1(i))}(g_i)(a_j)_{j\in\lambda_2})_{i\in\lambda_1}. \] \end{itemize} The class of all $M$-algebras is denoted by $\mathcal{V}(M)$. The category of $M$-algebras, that is, the class of objects is $\mathcal{V}(M)$ and the set of morphisms $A$ to $B$ is the set of all homomorphisms $A\rightarrow B$, is denoted by $\mathrm{Cat}(\mathcal{V}(M))$.
nodes.statement_short: An algebra of a many-sorted clone $M$: sorted sets with an action of $M$ compatible with composition; $\mathcal{V}(M)$ is the class and $\mathrm{Cat}(\mathcal{V}(M))$ the category.

nodes.name: Single-sorted clone
nodes.statement: The case $S$ is a singleton, $S$-sorted clone is simply called clone, or single-sorted clone.

nodes.name: Single-sorted projection notation $\pi_{(\lambda,i)}$
nodes.statement: In this case, the sort $(\lambda,v,s)$ is simply denoted by $\lambda$, $\lambda$-ary $i$-th projection is denoted by $\pi_{(\lambda,i)}$.

nodes.name: Clone of a type modulo an equational theory ${\cal M}_\kappa(F,E)$
nodes.statement: Let $S$ be a cardinal, $(F,E)$ be an $S$-sorted type with equational theory. Let $\kappa>S$ be an infinite cardinal. We define the $S$-sorted $<\mathclose\kappa$-ary clone of $F$ modulo $E$ as follows: \begin{itemize} \item The underlying set of a sort $(\lambda,v,s)$ is $T_{(\lambda,v,s)}/\mathclose\sim_E$ where $T_{(\lambda,v,s)}$ is the set of all $(\lambda,v)$-ary $s$-valued terms of $F$. The equivalence $t_1\sim_E t_2$ is defined by the condition \[ ``A\models E\Rightarrow A\models t_1=t_2\text{ for all } F\text{-algebra }A". \] \item Fundamental operations are defined as \begin{align*} \pi_i:=&x_i/\mathclose \sim_E, \\ c(t/\mathclose\sim_E,(u_i/\mathclose\sim_E)_{i\in\lambda}) :=&(t\circ (u_i)_{i\in \lambda})/\mathclose\sim_E. \end{align*} This clone is denoted by ${\cal M}_{\kappa}(F,E)$, or ${\cal M}_\kappa(\mathcal{V}_{(F,E)})$ by using the variety $\mathcal{V}_{(F,E)}$ defined by the equational theory $E$. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: The term clone ${\cal M}_\kappa(F,E)$: terms modulo the equivalence induced by $E$, with projections and substitution.

nodes.name: Definitional equivalence of varieties
nodes.statement: Let $S$ be a cardinal, $\kappa$ be an infinite cardinal and $\mathcal{V}_1,\mathcal{V}_2$ be $S$-sorted $<\mathclose\kappa$-ary varieties. The varieties $\mathcal{V}_1$ and $\mathcal{V}_2$ are said to be definitionally equivalent to each other if ${\cal M}_{\kappa}(\mathcal{V}_1)$ is isomorphic to ${\cal M}_\kappa(\mathcal{V}_2)$.

nodes.name: Correspondence between many-sorted varieties and clones
nodes.statement: Let $S$ be a non-zero cardinal, $\kappa>S$ be an infinite cardinal. \begin{enumerate} \item If $\mathcal{V}$ is an $S$-sorted $<\mathclose\kappa$-ary variety, then the clone ${\cal M}_\kappa(\mathcal{V})$ of terms of $\mathcal{V}$ is an $S$-sorted $<\mathclose\kappa$-ary clone. \item For an $S$-sorted $<\mathclose\kappa$-ary clone $M$, there exists an $S$-sorted $<\mathclose\kappa$-ary variety $\mathcal{V}$ such that ${\cal M}_{\kappa}(\mathcal{V})$ is isomorphic to $M$. \item Let $\kappa'>\kappa$ be a cardinal, $\mathcal{V}_1,\mathcal{V}_2$ be $S$-sorted $<\mathclose\kappa$-ary varieties. Then ${\cal M}_{\kappa'}(\mathcal{V}_1){\simeq}{\cal M}_{\kappa'}(\mathcal{V}_2)$ if and only if ${\cal M}_{\kappa}(\mathcal{V}_1){\simeq}{\cal M}_{\kappa}(\mathcal{V}_2)$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Term clones of $S$-sorted varieties are $S$-sorted clones, every such clone arises this way, and isomorphism of term clones does not depend on the arity bound.
assumptions: Let $S$ be a non-zero cardinal, $\kappa>S$ be an infinite cardinal.
conclusions: the clone ${\cal M}_\kappa(\mathcal{V})$ of terms of $\mathcal{V}$ is an $S$-sorted $<\mathclose\kappa$-ary clone.
there exists an $S$-sorted $<\mathclose\kappa$-ary variety $\mathcal{V}$ such that ${\cal M}_{\kappa}(\mathcal{V})$ is isomorphic to $M$.

nodes.name: Notation conventions for sorts and composition
nodes.statement: For simplification, we use, for example, the following variable notations through this paper: \begin{itemize} \item In the case $\lambda$ is finite, the sort $(\lambda,v,s)$ of many-sorted clone is denoted by $(v(0),\dots,v(\lambda-1))\rightarrow s$. The case $\lambda=1$, $(1,v,s)$ is denoted by $v(0)\rightarrow s$. The case $v$ is constant mapping, $v(i)=t$ for all $i$, $(n,v,s)$ is denoted by $nt\rightarrow s$. \item The composition operation $c$ of a clone is sometimes written as a composition of mappings. For example, $c(x,(y_i)_{i\in\lambda})$ is denoted by $x\circ(y_i)_{i\in\lambda}$ or $x(y_i)_{i\in \lambda}$. \item we write $(b,(a_s)_{s\in S\setminus\{s_0\}})$ the tuple $(x_s)_{s\in S}$ such that $x_{s_0}=b$ and $x_s=a_s$ for $s\in S$. The notation $((a_s)_{s\in T},(b_s)_{s\in S\setminus T})$ means the tuple $(x_s)_{s\in S}$ such that $x_s=a_s$ if $s\in T$ and $x_s=b_s$ if $s\in S\setminus T$. \item If we write $\pi_{(X,v,x)}\in M_{(X,v,s)}$, where $M$ is an $S$-sorted clone, $X$ is a set, $v:X\rightarrow S$, $s\in S$ and $x\in X$, we implicitly fix a bijection $\varphi:X\rightarrow |X|$ and $M_{(X,v,s)}$ is identified with $M_{(|X|,v\circ\varphi^{-1},s)}$ and $\pi_{(X,v,x)}$ means $\pi_{(|X|,v\circ \varphi^{-1},\varphi(x))}$. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Shorthand for finite sorts ($nt\rightarrow s$), composition written as $x\circ(y_i)$, tuple notation, and set-indexed projections.

nodes.name: Purity is necessary for a single-sorted counterpart
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{V}$ be a class of many-sorted algebras. If there is a class of single-sorted algebras naturally corresponding to $\mathcal{V}$, then all algebras in $\mathcal{V}$ have the property that the underlying sets of each sorts of the algebra are simultaneously empty or simultaneously non-empty. Here, ``naturally corresponding to $\mathcal{V}$" precisely means there is a natural equivalence between $\mathcal{V}$ and a single-sorted variety that is compatible with the natural equivalence described in Proposition \ref{pureset-and-sets}.
nodes.statement_short: A class of many-sorted algebras with a natural single-sorted counterpart must have all sorts simultaneously empty or non-empty.

nodes.name: Standing assumption on $S$ and $\kappa$
nodes.statement: Through this paper, $S$ be a fixed non-zero cardinal and $\kappa$ be a fixed infinite cardinal that $\kappa>S$.

nodes.name: Pure set and the category ${\bf Set}^S$
nodes.statement: \mbox{} \begin{enumerate} \item A family $(A_s)_{s\in S}$ of sets said to be pure if one of the following conditions holds: One condition is $A_s=\emptyset$ for all $s\in S$. The other is $A_s\neq \emptyset$ for all $s\in S$. \item Let $A=(A_s)_{s\in S}$ and $B=(B_s)_{s\in S}$ be pure sets. A morphism $f:A\rightarrow B$ of pure sets is a tuple $f=(f_s)_{s\in S}$ such that $f_s:A_s\rightarrow B_s$ for all $s\in S$. \item A category ${\textbf{{\rm Set}}}^S$ of $S$-sorted pure sets is the category that the class of objects consists of all $S$-sorted pure sets and the set of morphisms from a pure set $A$ to a pure set $B$ is the set of all morphisms of pure sets $A\rightarrow B$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: A family of sets is pure if all members are empty or all non-empty; ${\textbf{{\rm Set}}}^S$ is the category of $S$-sorted pure sets.
nodes.label: pure-set

nodes.name: Diagonal algebra of degree $S$
nodes.statement: The following single-sorted $<\mathclose\kappa$-ary clone $C_{{\cal D}_S}$ is called the clone corresponds to the variety of diagonal algebras of degree $S$: \begin{itemize} \item (Generators) $C_{{\cal D}_S}$ is generated by an element $d\in (C_{{\cal D}_S})_S$ of sort $S$. (Namely, $d$ is an $S$-ary term.) \item (Relations) The set of fundamental relations consists of the following only one equation, called diagonal identity: \[ d(d(\pi_{(S\times S,(s,t))})_{t\in S})_{s\in S}=d(\pi_{(S\times S,(s,s))})_{s\in S}. \] \end{itemize} A $C_{{\cal D}_S}$-algebra is called a diagonal algebra of degree $S$. The variety of diagonal algebras of degree $S$ is denoted by ${\cal D}_S$.
nodes.statement_short: The clone $C_{{\cal D}_S}$ generated by one $S$-ary operation $d$ subject to the diagonal identity; its algebras form the variety ${\cal D}_S$.

nodes.name: Equivalence of ${\bf Set}^S$ and diagonal algebras
nodes.statement: The category ${\textbf{{\rm Set}}}^S$ is categorically equivalent to the category ${\cal D}_S$ via the following categorical equivalence $\varphi$: \begin{itemize} \item (Objects correspondence) For $A=(A_s)_{s\in S}\in {\textbf{{\rm Set}}}^S$, $\varphi(A)$ is the following diagonal algebra: \begin{itemize} \item The underlying set is the product set $\prod_{s\in S}A_s$. \item For $(x_{s,t})_{t\in S}\in \prod_{t\in S}A_t$ ($s\in S$), the value of $d$ is defined as \[ d((x_{s,t})_{t\in S})_{s\in S}:=(x_{s,s})_{s\in S}. \] \end{itemize} \item (Morphism correspondence) For a morphism $f=(f_s)_{s\in S}:(A_s)_{s\in S}\rightarrow (B_s)_{s\in S}$ of pure set, the corresponding homomorphism $\varphi(f):\varphi((A_s)_{s\in S})\rightarrow \varphi((B_s)_{s\in S})$ is defined by $(x_s)_{s\in S}\mapsto (f_s(x_s))_{s\in S}$. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: The category of $S$-sorted pure sets is equivalent to the variety ${\cal D}_S$ via $A\mapsto\prod_s A_s$ with $d$ taking diagonals.
conclusions: The category ${\textbf{{\rm Set}}}^S$ is categorically equivalent to the category ${\cal D}_S$
nodes.label: pureset-and-sets

nodes.name: Concrete equivalence to a single-sorted variety
nodes.statement: Let $M$ be an $S$-sorted clone and consider the following condition: The variety of all $M$-algebras is concretely equivalent to a single-sorted variety, that is, categorically equivalent via a categorical equivalence that compatible with the categorical equivalence described in Proposition \ref{pureset-and-sets}.
nodes.statement_short: The variety of $M$-algebras is concretely equivalent to a single-sorted variety if they are categorically equivalent compatibly with ${\textbf{{\rm Set}}}^S\simeq{\cal D}_S$.

nodes.name: Concrete equivalence forces a pure clone
nodes.statement: This condition contains the condition that ``the underlying family of sets of an $M$-algebra is pure". The quoted condition is equivalent to that $M$ satisfies the next definition.
nodes.statement_short: Concrete equivalence requires underlying families of $M$-algebras to be pure, which is equivalent to $M$ being pure.
conclusions: The quoted condition is equivalent to that $M$ satisfies the next definition.

nodes.name: Pure clone
nodes.statement: An $S$-sorted clone $M$ is said to be pure if $M_{s_1\rightarrow s_2}\neq \emptyset$ for all $s_1,s_2\in S$.
nodes.label: pure-clone

nodes.name: Homogenization of a many-sorted clone ${\rm H}(M)$
nodes.statement: Let $M$ be an $S$-sorted $<\mathclose\kappa$-ary clone. A single-sorted $<\mathclose\kappa$-ary clone ${\rm H}(M)$ defined as follows is said a homogenization of $M$: \begin{itemize} \item (Underlying set) For a cardinal $\lambda<\kappa$, the underlying set ${\rm H}_\lambda(M)$ of a sort $\lambda$ (the sort corresponding to all $\lambda$-ary terms) consists of all tuple $(f_s)_{s\in S}$, where $f_s\in M_{(\lambda\times S,p_2,s)}$. Here, and through this paper, the symbol $p_2$ is used for the second projection of a product set. (In this case, $p_2$ is the mapping $(i,s')\mapsto s'$ from $\lambda\times S$ to $S$.) \item (Projection) The nullary operation $\pi_{(\lambda,i)}\in {\rm H}_\lambda(M)$ corresponds to $\lambda$-ary $i$-th projection is define as \[ \pi_{(\lambda,i)}:=(\pi_{(\lambda\times S,p_2,(i,s))})_{s\in S}. \] \item (Composition) For $f=(f_s)_{s\in S}\in {\rm H}_{\lambda_1}(M)$ and $g_i=(g_{i,s})_{s\in S}\in {\rm H}_{\lambda_2}(M)$ ($i\in \lambda_1$) the composition is defined as \[ c(f,(g_i)_{i\in\lambda_1}):=(c(f_s,(g_{i,t})_{(i,t)\in\lambda_1\times S}))_{s\in S}. \] \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: ${\rm H}(M)$ has as $\lambda$-ary elements the $S$-tuples of terms in $M_{(\lambda\times S,p_2,s)}$, with componentwise projections and composition.
nodes.label: homog-clone

nodes.name: Homogenization of an algebra ${\rm H}(A)$
nodes.statement: Let $M$ be an $S$-sorted $<\mathclose\kappa$-ary clone. Let $A=(A_s)_{s\in S}$ be an $M$-algebra. We define the homogenization ${\rm H}(A)$ of $A$ as the following ${\rm H}(M)$-algebra: \begin{itemize} \item The underlying set is $\prod_{s\in S}A_s$. \item The action of $f=(f_s)_{s\in S}\in {\rm H}_\lambda(M)$ is \[ ((a_{i,t})_{t\in S})_{i\in\lambda}\mapsto (f_s(a_{i,t})_{(i,t)\in\lambda\times S})_{s\in S}. \] \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: ${\rm H}(A)$ is the ${\rm H}(M)$-algebra on $\prod_s A_s$ with componentwise action.
nodes.label: homog-alg

nodes.name: ${\rm H}(A)$ is an ${\rm H}(M)$-algebra
nodes.statement: Let $M$ and $A$ be as Definition \ref{homog-alg}. Then ${\rm H}(A)$ is actually ${\rm H}(M)$-algebra. Namely, the compatibility condition \[ f(g_i(a_j)_{j\in\lambda_2})_{i\in\lambda_1} =c(f,(g_i)_{i\in \lambda_1})(a_j)_{j\in\lambda_2} \] holds for $\lambda_1,\lambda_2<\kappa$, $f\in {\rm H}_{\lambda_1}(M)$, $g_i\in{\rm H}_{\lambda_2}(M)$ ($i\in \lambda_1$) and $a_j\in {\rm H}(A)$ ($j\in \lambda_2$).
assumptions: Let $M$ and $A$ be as Definition \ref{homog-alg}.
conclusions: Then ${\rm H}(A)$ is actually ${\rm H}(M)$-algebra.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3.4
nodes.statement: Let $f=(f_s)_{s\in S}$, $g_i=(g_{i,s})_{s\in S}$ and $a_j=(a_{j,s})_{s\in S}$. Then \begin{align*} f(g_i(a_j)_{j\in\lambda_2})_{i\in\lambda_1} &=f((g_{i,t}(a_{j,u})_{(j,u)\in\lambda_2\times S})_{t\in S})_{i\in\lambda_1}\\ &=(f_s(g_{i,t}(a_{j,u})_{(j,u)\in\lambda_2\times S}) _{(i,t)\in\lambda_1\times S})_{s\in S}\\ &=(c(f_s,(g_{i,t})_{(i,t)\in\lambda_1\times S}) (a_{j,u})_{(j,u)\in\lambda_2\times S})_{s\in S}\\ &=c(f,(g_i)_{i\in \lambda_1})(a_j)_{j\in\lambda_2}. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Direct computation unfolding the componentwise action and composition.

nodes.name: Homogenization is a functor
nodes.statement: Let $M$ be an $S$-sorted $<\mathclose\kappa$-ary clone, $A,B$ be $M$-algebras, and $\varphi:A\rightarrow B$ be a homomorphism of $M$-algebras. Then ${\rm H}(\varphi):(a_s)_{s\in S}\mapsto (\varphi_s(a_s))_{s\in S}$ is a homomorphism ${\rm H}(A)\rightarrow {\rm H}(B)$ of ${\rm H}(M)$-algebras. Furthermore, the following correspondence ${\rm H}$ is a functor from the category $\mathrm{Cat}(\mathcal{V}(M))$ of $M$-algebras to the category $\mathrm{Cat}(\mathcal{V}({\rm H}(M)))$ of ${\rm H}(M)$-algebras: \begin{itemize} \item (Object correspondence) $A\mapsto {\rm H}(A)$. \item (Morphism correspondence) $\varphi\mapsto {\rm H}(\varphi)$. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Homomorphisms of $M$-algebras induce homomorphisms of homogenizations, making ${\rm H}$ a functor $\mathrm{Cat}(\mathcal{V}(M))\to\mathrm{Cat}(\mathcal{V}({\rm H}(M)))$.
assumptions: Let $M$ be an $S$-sorted $<\mathclose\kappa$-ary clone, $A,B$ be $M$-algebras, and $\varphi:A\rightarrow B$ be a homomorphism of $M$-algebras.
conclusions: Then ${\rm H}(\varphi):(a_s)_{s\in S}\mapsto (\varphi_s(a_s))_{s\in S}$ is a homomorphism ${\rm H}(A)\rightarrow {\rm H}(B)$ of ${\rm H}(M)$-algebras.
the following correspondence ${\rm H}$ is a functor
nodes.label: many-single

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3.5
nodes.statement: Let $f=(f_s)_{s\in S}\in {\rm H}_\lambda(M)$ and $a_i=(a_{i,s})_{s\in S}$ for $i\in\lambda$. Then \begin{align*} {\rm H}(\varphi)(f(a_i)_{i\in\lambda}) &={\rm H}(\varphi)(f_s(a_{i,t})_{(i,t)\in\lambda\times S})_{s\in S}\\ &=(\varphi_s f_s(a_{i,t})_{(i,t)\in\lambda\times S})_{s\in S}\\ &=(f_s(\varphi_t(a_{i,t}))_{(i,t)\in\lambda\times S})_{s\in S}\\ &=f({\rm H}(\varphi)(a_i))_{i\in\lambda}. \end{align*} The correspondence ${\rm H}$ being a functor means \[ {\rm H}(\mathrm{id}_A)=\mathrm{id}_{{\rm H}(A)} \] holds for all $A\in\mathcal{V}(M)$, and \[ {\rm H}(\psi)\circ{\rm H}(\varphi)={\rm H}(\psi\circ\varphi) \] hold for all homomorphisms $\psi,\varphi$ that ${\rm cod}(\varphi)={\rm dom}(\psi)$. It is easily verified.
nodes.statement_short: Componentwise computation shows ${\rm H}(\varphi)$ commutes with operations; functoriality is routine.

nodes.name: Homogenization of a pure clone has diagonal terms
nodes.statement: Let $M$ be an $S$-sorted $<\mathclose\kappa$-ary pure clone. Assume $d\in {\rm H}_S(M)$ and $e_s\in {\rm H}_1(M)$ ($s\in S$) be terms satisfying the following conditions: \begin{itemize} \item $d$ is defined as $d=(\pi_{(S\times S,p_2,(s,s))})_{s\in S}$. (Intuitively, the term operation of $d$ acts as \[ A^S\ni ((a_{s,t})_{t\in S})_{s\in S}\mapsto (a_{s,s})_{s\in S}\in A \] for each ${\rm H}(M)$-algebra $A$.) \item Each term $e_s$ satisfies follows: \begin{itemize} \item $e_s\circ(\pi_{(S,\mathrm{id}_S,s)},(x_u)_{u\in S\setminus\{s\}})=e_s$ (Intuitively, the value of term operation $e_s(a_u)_{u\in S}$ depends only on $s$-component $a_s$.) \item If $e_s=(e_{s,t})_{t\in S}$, where $e_{s,t}\in M_{(S,\mathrm{id}_S,t)}$, then $e_{s,s}=\pi_{(S,\mathrm{id}_S,s)}$. (Intuitively, the value $e_{s,s}(a_u)_{u\in S}$ of $s$-component is $a_s$.) \end{itemize} \end{itemize} Then the following equations hold in ${\rm H}(M)$. \begin{enumerate} \item $e_s\circ d=e_s\circ \pi_{(S,s)}$. \item $d\circ(e_s\circ \pi_{(S,s)})_{s\in S}=d$. \item $d\circ (\pi_{(S,0)})_{s\in S}=\pi_{(S,0)}$, where $0\in S$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: In ${\rm H}(M)$ for pure $M$, the diagonal term $d$ and suitable unary terms $e_s$ satisfy the three diagonal-pair identities.
assumptions: Let $M$ be an $S$-sorted $<\mathclose\kappa$-ary pure clone.
conclusions: $e_s\circ d=e_s\circ \pi_{(S,s)}$.
$d\circ(e_s\circ \pi_{(S,s)})_{s\in S}=d$.
$d\circ (\pi_{(S,0)})_{s\in S}=\pi_{(S,0)}$, where $0\in S$.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3.6
nodes.statement: 1. \begin{align*} e_s\circ d =&e_s\circ (\pi_{(S\times S,p_2,(t,t))}^M)_{t\in S}&\\ =&e_s\circ (\pi_{(S\times S,p_2,(s,t))}^M)_{t\in S}&(e_s\text{ depends only on }s\text{-componet})\\ =&e_s\circ \pi_{(S,s)}^{{\rm H}(M)}.& \end{align*} Here and through the proof of this proposition, $\pi^M$ and $\pi^{{\rm H}(M)}$ denote projection constants of $M$ and ${\rm H}(M)$ respectively. 2. \begin{align*} d\circ (e_s\circ \pi_{(S,s)}^{{\rm H}(M)})_{s\in S} =& (\pi_{(S\times S,p_2,(s,s))}^M)_{s\in S} \circ ((e_{s,t})_{t\in S}\circ (\pi_{(S\times S,p_2,(s,u))}^M)_{u\in S})_{s\in S}\\ =& (e_{s,s}\circ (\pi_{(S\times S,p_2,(s,u))}^M)_{u\in S})_{s\in S}\\ =& (\pi_{(S\times S,p_2,(s,s))}^M)_{s\in S}\\ =& d. \end{align*} 3. \begin{align*} d\circ (\pi_{(S,0)}^{{\rm H}(M)})_{s\in S} =&(\pi_{(S\times S,p_2,(s,s))}^M)_{s\in S} \circ (\pi_{(S\times S,p_2,(0,t))}^M)_{(s,t)\in S\times S}\\ =& (\pi_{(S\times S,p_2,(0,s))}^M)_{s\in S}\\ =& \pi_{(S,0)}^{{\rm H}(M)}. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Verify each of the three identities by direct computation with projections of $M$.

nodes.name: $S$-ary diagonal pair
nodes.statement: Let $C$ be a single-sorted $<\mathclose\kappa$-ary clone. The tuple $(d,(e_s)_{s\in S})\in C_S\times C_1{}^S$ is said an $S$-ary diagonal pair of $C$ if the following equations holds: \begin{enumerate} \item $e_{s}\circ d=\pi_{(S,s)}$ for all $s\in S$. \item $d(e_s\circ \pi_{(S,s)})_{s\in S}=d$. \item $d(\pi_{(S,0)})_{s\in S}=\pi_{(S,0)}$ for $0\in S$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.label: diagonal-pair

nodes.name: Diagonal pair satisfies the diagonal identity
nodes.statement: If $(d,(e_s)_{s\in S})$ is a diagonal pair of a clone $C$, then $d$ satisfies diagonal identity \[ d(d(\pi_{(S\times S,(s,t))})_{t\in S})_{s\in S} =d(\pi_{(S\times S,(s,s))})_{s\in S}. \] Namely, $C$-algebras have diagonal algebras reduct.
nodes.statement_short: The $d$ of a diagonal pair satisfies the diagonal identity, so $C$-algebras have diagonal-algebra reducts.
assumptions: If $(d,(e_s)_{s\in S})$ is a diagonal pair of a clone $C$,
conclusions: then $d$ satisfies diagonal identity
Namely, $C$-algebras have diagonal algebras reduct.

nodes.name: Proof of Remark 3.8
nodes.statement: \begin{align*} d(d(\pi_{(S\times S,(s,t))})_{t\in S})_{s\in S} =&d(e_sd(\pi_{(S\times S,(s,t))})_{t\in S})_{s\in S}\\ =&d(e_s\pi_{(S\times S,(s,s))})_{s\in S}\\ =&d(\pi_{(S\times S,(s,s))})_{s\in S}. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Insert $e_s$ via the identity $d(e_s\pi_{(S,s)})=d$ and collapse with $e_s\circ d=\pi_{(S,s)}$.

nodes.name: Idempotent retract and matrix product of a clone
nodes.statement: Let $C$ be a single-sorted $<\mathclose\kappa$-clone. \begin{enumerate} \item Let $e\in C_1$ be an idempotent element, namely, $e$ satisfies $e\circ e=e$. An idempotent retract, denoted by $e(C)$, of $C$ by $e$ is the following $<\mathclose\kappa$-ary clone. \begin{itemize} \item (Underlying set) The underlying set $e(C)_{\lambda}$ of the sort $\lambda<\kappa$ is $\{f\in C_\lambda\mid e\circ f=f\}/\mathclose\sim_\lambda$, where $\sim_\lambda$ is the equivalence relation defined as $f\sim_\lambda g :\Leftrightarrow f\circ (e\pi_{(\lambda,i)})_{i\in\lambda}=g\circ (e\pi_{(\lambda,i)})_{i\in\lambda}$. \item (Projection) The $\lambda$-ary $i$-th projection $\pi^{e(C)}_{(\lambda,i)}$ is $e\circ \pi^C_{(\lambda,i)}\mathclose/\mathclose\sim_\lambda$, where $\pi^C_{(\lambda,i)}$ is the $\lambda$-ary $i$-th projection of $C$. \item (Composition) For $f\mathclose/\mathclose\sim_{\lambda_1}\in e(C)_{\lambda_1}$ and $g_i\mathclose/\mathclose\sim_{\lambda_2}\in C(C)_{\lambda_2}$ ($i\in\lambda_1$), we define \[ c^{e(C)}(f\mathclose/\mathclose\sim_{\lambda_1},(g_i\mathclose/\mathclose\sim_{\lambda_2})_{i\in\lambda_1}) :=c^C(f,(g_i)_{i\in\lambda_1})\mathclose/\mathclose\sim_{\lambda_2}, \] where $c^C$ is the composition operation of $C$. \end{itemize} \item Let $(e_s)_{s\in S}\in C_1{}^S$ be a family of idempotent elements. The matrix product $\boxtimes_{s\in S}e_s(C)$ of a family of idempotent retracts $(e_s(C))_{s\in S}$ is defined as the following $<\mathclose\kappa$-ary clone: \begin{itemize} \item (Underlying set) The underlying set $(\boxtimes_{s\in S}e(C))_{\lambda}$ of the sort $\lambda<\kappa$ is \[ \{(f_s/\mathclose\sim_{\lambda})_{s\in S}\in (C_{\lambda\times S}/\mathclose\sim_{\lambda})^S \mid \forall s\in S;e_sf_s=f_s\}, \] where the equivalence $\sim_\lambda$ is defined as \[ f\sim_{\lambda} g:\Longleftrightarrow f\circ (e_t\pi_{(\lambda\times S,(i,t))})_{(i,t)\in\lambda\times S} =g\circ (e_t\pi_{(\lambda\times S,(i,t))})_{(i,t)\in\lambda\times S}. \] \item (Projection) The $\lambda$-ary $i$-th projection $\pi_{(\lambda,i)}$ is defined by $(e_s\circ \pi^{C}_{\lambda\times S,(i,s)}\mathclose/\mathclose\sim_\lambda)_{s\in S}$, where $\pi_{(\lambda\times S,(i,s))}^C$ is the $\lambda\times S$-ary $(i,s)$-th projection constant of $C$. \item (Composition) For $f=(f_s\mathclose/\mathclose\sim_{\lambda_1})_{s\in S}\in (\boxtimes_{s\in S}e(C))_{\lambda_1}$ and $g_i=(g_{i,s}\mathclose/\mathclose\sim_{\lambda_2})_{s\in S}\in (\boxtimes_{s\in S}e(C))_{\lambda_2}$ ($i\in\lambda_1$), the composition is defined by \[ c(f,(g_i)_{i\in\lambda_1}) :=(c^C(f_s,(g_{i,t})_{(i,t)\in\lambda_1\times S})\mathclose/\mathclose\sim_{\lambda_2})_{s\in S}, \] where $c^C$ is the composition operation of $C$. \end{itemize} \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: The idempotent retract $e(C)$ of a clone by an idempotent $e$, and the matrix product $\boxtimes_{s\in S}e_s(C)$ of a family of idempotent retracts.

nodes.name: Idempotent retract and matrix product of an algebra
nodes.statement: Let $C$ be a $<\mathclose\kappa$-ary clone, $A$ be a $C$-algebra. \begin{enumerate} \item Let $e\in C_1$ be an idempotent element. The idempotent retract (in literature e.g. \cite{Iza},\cite{Kea}, this is referred as a neighbourhood) of $A$ by $e$, denoted by $e(A)$, is defined as the following $e(C)$-algebra: \begin{itemize} \item The underlying set is $e(A)=\{e(a)\mid a\in A\}$. \item The action of $f\mathclose/\mathclose\sim_\lambda\in (e(C))_{\lambda}$ is $(a_i)_{i\in\lambda}\mapsto f(a_i)_{i\in\lambda}$. \end{itemize} \item Let $(e_s)_{s\in S}$ be a family of idempotent elements of $C$. The matrix product $\boxtimes_{s\in S}e_s(A)$ is defined as the following $\boxtimes_{s\in S}e_s(C)$-algebra: \begin{itemize} \item The underlying set is $\prod_{s\in S}e_s(A)$. \item The action of $(f_s\mathclose/\mathclose\sim_\lambda)_{s\in S}\in (\boxtimes_{s\in S}e_s(C))_\lambda$ is \[ ((a_{i,t})_{t\in S})_{i\in\lambda}\mapsto (f_s(a_{i,t})_{(i,t)\in\lambda\times S})_{s\in S}. \] \end{itemize} \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: The $e(C)$-algebra $e(A)$ and the $\boxtimes_{s}e_s(C)$-algebra $\prod_s e_s(A)$ with componentwise action.

nodes.name: Matrix product of algebras is a functor
nodes.statement: Let $C$ be a $<\mathclose\kappa$-ary clone and $(e_s)_{s\in S}$ be a family of idempotent elements of $C$. Let $A$ and $B$ be $C$-algebras, $\varphi:A\rightarrow B$ be a homomorphism of $C$-algebras. Then the mapping \mbox{$\tilde{\varphi}:\boxtimes_{s\in S}e_s(A)\rightarrow \boxtimes_{s\in S}e_s(B)$} defined as $(a_s)_{s\in S}\mapsto (\varphi(a_s))_{s\in S}$ is a homomorphism of $\boxtimes_{s\in S}e_s(C)$-algebras. Furthermore, the (pair of) correspondence $A\mapsto \boxtimes_{s\in S}e_s(A)$ and $\varphi\mapsto \tilde{\varphi}$ is a functor $\mathcal{V}(C)\rightarrow \mathcal{V}(\boxtimes_{s\in S}e_s(C))$.
assumptions: Let $C$ be a $<\mathclose\kappa$-ary clone and $(e_s)_{s\in S}$ be a family of idempotent elements of $C$.
Let $A$ and $B$ be $C$-algebras, $\varphi:A\rightarrow B$ be a homomorphism of $C$-algebras.
conclusions: is a homomorphism of $\boxtimes_{s\in S}e_s(C)$-algebras.
is a functor $\mathcal{V}(C)\rightarrow \mathcal{V}(\boxtimes_{s\in S}e_s(C))$.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 4.3
nodes.statement: Let $f=(f_s\mathclose/\mathclose\sim_\lambda)_{s\in S}\in (\boxtimes_{s\in S}e_s(C))_{\lambda}$ and $a_{i}=(a_{i,s})_{s\in S}\in \boxtimes_{s\in S}e_s(A)$ for $i\in\lambda$. Then \begin{align*} \tilde{\varphi}(f(a_i)_{i\in\lambda}) &=(\varphi(f_s(a_{i,t})_{(i,t)\in\lambda\times S}))_{s\in S}\\ &=(f_s(\varphi(a_{i,t}))_{(i,t)\in\lambda\times S})_{s\in S}\\ &=f(\tilde{\varphi}(a_i))_{i\in\lambda}. \end{align*} The correspondence $\varphi\mapsto \tilde{\varphi}$ clearly preserves identity morphisms and composition. Thus the correspondence is a functor.
nodes.statement_short: Direct computation that $\tilde\varphi$ commutes with the componentwise action; functoriality is clear.

nodes.name: Matrix product has a diagonal pair
nodes.statement: Let $C$ be a single-sorted $<\mathclose\kappa$-ary clone, $(e_s)_{s\in S}$ be a family of idempotent elements of $C$. Let $d\in (\boxtimes_{s\in S} e_s(C))_{S}$ and $\tilde{e}_s\in (\boxtimes_{s\in S} e_s(C))_1$ be the terms defined as follows: \begin{align*} d&:=(e_s\circ \pi_{(S\times S,(s,s))}\mathclose/\mathclose\sim_S)_{s\in S},\\ \tilde{e}_s&:=(e_t\circ \pi_{(S,s)}\mathclose/\mathclose\sim_1)_{t\in S}. \end{align*} Then $(d,(\tilde{e}_s)_{s\in S})$ is a diagonal pair of $\boxtimes_{s\in S}e_s(C)$.
nodes.statement_short: The matrix product $\boxtimes_s e_s(C)$ has an explicit diagonal pair built from the idempotents and diagonal projections.
assumptions: Let $C$ be a single-sorted $<\mathclose\kappa$-ary clone, $(e_s)_{s\in S}$ be a family of idempotent elements of $C$.
conclusions: Then $(d,(\tilde{e}_s)_{s\in S})$ is a diagonal pair of $\boxtimes_{s\in S}e_s(C)$.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 4.4
nodes.statement: $d,\tilde{e}_s\in\boxtimes_{t\in S} e_t(C)$ immediately follows from the definition. In the proof of this proposition, we write $\pi^C$/$\pi^{\boxtimes e(C)}$ the projection terms of $C$/$\boxtimes_{s\in S}e_s(C)$ respectively. 1. \begin{align*} \tilde{e}_s\circ d =& \tilde{e}_s\circ (e_t\circ \pi_{(S\times S,(t,t))}^C)_{t\in S}&\\ =& \tilde{e}_s\circ (e_t\circ \pi_{(S\times S,(s,t))}^C)_{t\in S}& (\tilde{e}_s\text{ depends only on }s\text{-component})\\ =&\tilde{e}_s\circ \pi_{(S,s)}^{\boxtimes e(C)}.& \end{align*} 2. \begin{align*} d\circ (\tilde{e}_s\circ \pi_{(S,s)}^{\boxtimes e(C)})_{s\in S} =& (e_t\circ \pi_{(S\times S,(t,t))}^C)_{t\in S} \circ ((e_t\pi_{(S,s)}^C)_{t\in S} \circ (\pi_{(S\times S,(s,t))}^C)_{t\in S})_{s\in S}\\ =& (e_t\circ \pi_{(S\times S,(t,t))}^C)_{t\in S} \circ ((e_t\pi_{(S\times S,(s,s))}^C)_{t\in S})_{s\in S}\\ =& (e_t\circ e_t\pi_{(S\times S,(t,t))}^C)_{t\in S}\\ =& (e_t\circ \pi_{(S\times S,(t,t))}^C)_{t\in S}\\ =& d. \end{align*} 3. \begin{align*} d\circ (\pi_{(S,0)}^{\boxtimes e(C)})_{s\in S} =& (e_t\circ \pi_{(S\times S,(t,t))}^C)_{t\in S} \circ ((e_t\circ \pi_{(S\times S,(0,t))}^C)_{t\in S})_{s\in S}\\ =& (e_t\circ (e_t\circ \pi_{(S\times S,(0,t))}^C))_{t\in S}\\ =& (e_t\circ \pi_{(S\times S,(0,t))}^C)_{t\in S}\\ =& \pi_{(S,0)}^{\boxtimes e(C)}. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Verify the three diagonal-pair identities by direct computation using idempotency of the $e_t$.

nodes.name: Decomposition of a clone with a diagonal pair as a matrix product
nodes.statement: Let $C$ be a single-sorted clone, $(d,(e_s)_{s\in S})$ be a diagonal pair. Then the clone $C$ is isomorphic to $\boxtimes_{s\in S}e_s(C)$.
nodes.statement_short: A single-sorted clone with a diagonal pair $(d,(e_s))$ is isomorphic to the matrix product $\boxtimes_s e_s(C)$.
assumptions: Let $C$ be a single-sorted clone, $(d,(e_s)_{s\in S})$ be a diagonal pair.
conclusions: Then the clone $C$ is isomorphic to $\boxtimes_{s\in S}e_s(C)$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4.5
nodes.statement: Suppose $(d,(e_s)_{s\in S})$ is a diagonal pair of $C$. We define $\varphi_\lambda:C_\lambda\rightarrow (\boxtimes_{s\in S}e_s(C))_\lambda$ as \[ \varphi_\lambda:f\mapsto (e_s\circ f\circ (d\circ(\pi_{(\lambda\times S,(i,t))})_{t\in S}) _{i\in\lambda}/\mathclose\sim_\lambda)_{s\in \lambda}. \] Note that $\varphi_{\lambda}(f)\in (\boxtimes_{s\in S}e_s(C))_\lambda$ follows from $e_s\circ e_s=e_s$. We prove injectivity of $\varphi_\lambda$. Let $f,g\in C_\lambda$ and assume $\varphi_\lambda(f)=\varphi_\lambda(g)$, namely, assume the equality \begin{align*} &e_sf\circ(d\circ(e_t\pi_{(\lambda\times S,(i,t))})_{t\in S})_{i\in\lambda}\\ =&e_sf\circ (d\circ (\pi_{(\lambda\times S,(i,t))})_{t\in S})_{i\in\lambda} \circ (e_t\pi_{(\lambda\times S,(i,t))})_{(i,t)\in\lambda\times S}\\ =&e_sg\circ (d\circ (\pi_{(\lambda\times S,(i,t))})_{t\in S})_{i\in\lambda} \circ (e_t\pi_{(\lambda\times S,(i,t))})_{(i,t)\in\lambda\times S}\\ =&e_sg\circ(d\circ(e_t\pi_{(\lambda\times S,(i,t))})_{t\in S})_{i\in\lambda} \end{align*} hold for all $s\in S$. Then \begin{align*} f =&d\circ (e_s)_{s\in S}\circ f\circ (\pi_{(\lambda,i)})_{i\in\lambda}\\ =&d\circ (e_s)_{s\in S}\circ f\circ (d\circ (\pi_{(\lambda,i)})_{t\in S})_{i\in\lambda}\\ =&d\circ (e_s)_{s\in S}\circ f\circ (d\circ (\pi_{(\lambda\times S,(i,t))})_{t\in S})_{i\in\lambda} \circ (\pi_{(\lambda,i)})_{(i,t)\in\lambda\times S}\\ =&d\circ (e_s)_{s\in S}\circ f\circ (d\circ (e_t\pi_{(\lambda\times S,(i,t))})_{t\in S})_{i\in\lambda} \circ (\pi_{(\lambda,i)})_{(i,t)\in\lambda\times S}\\ =&d\circ (e_s)_{s\in S}\circ g\circ (d\circ (e_t\pi_{(\lambda\times S,(i,t))})_{t\in S})_{i\in\lambda} \circ (\pi_{(\lambda,i)})_{(i,t)\in\lambda\times S}\\ =&g. \end{align*} Next, we prove surjectivity of $\varphi_\lambda$. Let $(f_s\mathclose/\mathclose\sim_{\lambda})_{s\in S}\in(\boxtimes_{s\in S}e_s(C))_\lambda$. We define $\tilde{f}\in C_\lambda$ as \[ \tilde{f}:=d\circ (f_s)_{s\in S}\circ (e_t\pi_{(\lambda,i)})_{(i,t)\in\lambda\times S}. \] Then \begin{align*} \varphi_{\lambda}(\tilde{f}) =&\left(e_sd\circ (f_t)_{t\in S} \circ (e_t\pi_{(\lambda,i)})_{(i,t)\in\lambda\times S} \circ (d\circ (\pi_{(\lambda\times S,(i,u))})_{u\in S})_{i\in\lambda}\mathclose/\mathclose\sim_{\lambda}\right)_{s\in S}\\ =&\left(e_sf_s \circ (e_td\circ (\pi_{(\lambda\times S,(i,u))})_{u\in S})_{(i,t)\in\lambda\times S}\mathclose/\mathclose\sim_{\lambda}\right)_{s\in S}\\ =&\left(f_s \circ (e_t\pi_{(\lambda\times S,(i,t))})_{(i,t)\in\lambda\times S}\mathclose/\mathclose\sim_{\lambda}\right)_{s\in S}\\ =&(f_s\mathclose/\mathclose\sim_{\lambda})_{s\in S}. \end{align*} Finally, we prove $\varphi=(\varphi_{\lambda})_{\lambda<\kappa}$ is a homomorphism. Let $\lambda_1,\lambda_2<\kappa$ and $f\in C_{\lambda_1}$, $g_i\in C_{\lambda_2}$ for $i\in\lambda_1$. Then \begin{align*} &\varphi_{\lambda_2}(f\circ (g_i)_{i\in\lambda_1})\\ =&\left(e_s f\circ (g_i)_{i\in\lambda_1} \circ (d\circ (\pi_{(\lambda_2\times S,(j,t))})_{t\in S})_{j\in\lambda_2}\mathclose/\mathclose\sim_{\lambda_2}\right)_{s\in S}\\ =&\left(e_sf\circ (d\circ (g_i)_{u\in S})_{i\in\lambda_1} \circ (d\circ (\pi_{(\lambda_2\times S,(j,t))})_{t\in S})_{j\in\lambda_2}\mathclose/\mathclose\sim_{\lambda_2}\right)_{s\in S}\\ =&\left(e_s f\circ (d\circ (e_ug_i)_{u\in S})_{i\in\lambda_1} \circ (d\circ (\pi_{(\lambda_2\times S,(j,t))})_{t\in S})_{j\in\lambda_2}\mathclose/\mathclose\sim_{\lambda_2}\right)_{s\in S}\\ =&\left(e_s f\circ (d\circ (\pi_{(\lambda_1\times S,(i,u))})_{u\in S})_{i\in\lambda_1} \circ (e_ug_i)_{(i,u)\in\lambda_1\times S} \circ (d\circ (\pi_{(\lambda_2\times S,(j,t))})_{t\in S})_{j\in\lambda_2}\mathclose/\mathclose\sim_{\lambda_2}\right)_{s\in S}\\ =&\left(e_s f\circ (d\circ (\pi_{(\lambda_1\times S,(i,u))})_{u\in S})_{i\in\lambda_1}\mathclose/\mathclose\sim_{\lambda_1}\right)_{s\in S} \circ \left(e_ug_i \circ (d\circ (\pi_{(\lambda_2\times S,(j,t))})_{t\in S})_{j\in\lambda_2}\mathclose/\mathclose\sim_{\lambda_2}\right)_{(i,u)\in \lambda_1\times S}\\ =&\varphi_{\lambda_1}(f)\circ (\varphi_{\lambda_2}(g_i))_{i\in\lambda_1}. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Construct an explicit map $\varphi_\lambda$ via $e_s$ and $d$, then prove it injective, surjective (explicit preimage) and a clone homomorphism. The key identity is $f=d\circ(e_s)\circ f$ from the diagonal-pair axioms.

nodes.name: Heterogenization clone $C_{(d,(e_s)_{s\in S})}$
nodes.statement: Let $C$ be a single-sorted $<\mathclose\kappa$-ary clone. Assume $C$ has an $S$-ary diagonal pair $(d,(e_s)_{s\in S})$. We define an $S$-sorted $<\mathclose\kappa$-ary clone $C_{(d,(e_s)_{s\in S})}$ as follows: \begin{itemize} \item (Underlying set) For $\lambda<\kappa$, $v:\lambda\rightarrow S$ and $s\in S$, the underlying set of the sort $(\lambda,v,t)$ is \[ C_{(d,(e_s)_{s\in S}),(\lambda,v,t)} :=\{f\in C_\lambda\mid e_tf=f\}/\mathclose\sim_{\lambda,v}, \] where the equivalence $\sim_{\lambda,v}$ is defined as \begin{align*} f\sim_{\lambda,v} g &:\Longleftrightarrow f\circ (e_{v(i)}\circ \pi_{(\lambda,i)})_{i\in\lambda} =g\circ (e_{v(i)}\circ \pi_{(\lambda,i)})_{i\in\lambda}. \end{align*} \item (Projection) For $\lambda<\kappa$, $v:\lambda\rightarrow S$ and $i\in\lambda$, the projection constant $\pi_{(\lambda,v,i)}$ is defined as $e_{v(i)}\circ \pi_{(\lambda,i)}\mathclose/\mathclose\sim_{\lambda,v}$. \item (Composition) For $\lambda_k<\kappa$, $v:\lambda_k\rightarrow S$ ($k=1,2$) and $s\in S$, the composition operation \begin{align*} c_{(\lambda_1,v_1,s),(\lambda_2,v_2)}:& C_{(d,(e_s)_{s\in S}),(\lambda_1,v_1,s)}\times \prod_{i\in \lambda_1}C_{((d,(e_s)_{s\in S}),(\lambda_2,v_2,v_1(i))}\\ \rightarrow & C_{(d,(e_s)_{s\in S}),(\lambda_2,v_2,s)} \end{align*} is defined by $(f/\mathclose\sim_{\lambda_1,v_1},(g_i/\mathclose\sim_{\lambda_2,v_2})_{i\in\lambda_1}) \mapsto (f\circ(g_i)_{i\in\lambda_1})/\mathclose\sim_{\lambda_2,v_2}$. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: From a clone $C$ with diagonal pair, the $S$-sorted clone whose $(\lambda,v,t)$ sort is $\{f: e_tf=f\}$ modulo agreement after precomposing with $e_{v(i)}$.
nodes.label: heterogenization-clone

nodes.name: Heterogenization of an algebra $A_{(d,(e_s)_{s\in S})}$
nodes.statement: Let $C$ be a $<\mathclose\kappa$-ary clone that has a diagonal pair $(d,(e_s)_{s\in S})$. Let $A$ be a $C$-algebra. We define a $C_{(d,(e_s)_{s\in S})}$-algebra $A_{(d,(e_s)_{s\in S})}$ as follows: \begin{itemize} \item (Underlying set) The underlying set $A_{(d,(e_s)_{s\in S}),s}$ of the sort $s\in S$ is $e_s(A)$. \item (Action of $C_{(d,(e_s)_{s\in S})}$) A term $f/\mathclose\sim_{\lambda,v}\in C_{(d,(e_s)_{s\in S}),(\lambda,v,s)}$ acts as \[ \prod_{i\in\lambda} A_{(d,(e_s)_{s\in S}),v(i)}\ni(a_i)_{i\in\lambda} \mapsto f(a_i)_{i\in\lambda}\in A_{(d,(e_s)_{s\in S}),s}. \] \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: The $C_{(d,(e_s))}$-algebra whose sort $s$ is $e_s(A)$, with terms acting as in $A$.

nodes.name: Normalized representatives in the heterogenization
nodes.statement: In the Definition \ref{heterogenization-clone}, $g:=f\circ (e_{v(i)}\circ \pi_{(\lambda,i)})_{i\in\lambda}\sim_{\lambda,v} f$ holds for $f\in C_\lambda$. Moreover $g$ satisfy $g\circ (e_{v(i)}\circ \pi_{(\lambda,i)})_{i\in\lambda}=g$. Thus for any element $\tilde{f}$ of $C_{(d,(e_s)_{s\in S}),(\lambda,v,t)}$, we can choose a term $g\in C_\lambda$ that satisfies $g\circ (e_{v(i)}\circ \pi_{(\lambda,i)})_{i\in\lambda}=g$ as a representative for $\tilde{f}$.
nodes.statement_short: Every element of a heterogenization sort has a representative $g$ fixed by precomposition with $(e_{v(i)}\pi_{(\lambda,i)})_i$.
nodes.label: hetero-representative

nodes.name: Idempotents of diagonal pairs with the same $d$ absorb
nodes.statement: Let $C$ be a single-sorted $<\mathclose\kappa$-ary clone and ${(d,(e_s)_{s\in S})}$, ${(d,(e'_s)_{s\in S})}$ be diagonal pairs of $C$. Then $e_se'_s=e_s$ holds for $s\in S$.
assumptions: Let $C$ be a single-sorted $<\mathclose\kappa$-ary clone and ${(d,(e_s)_{s\in S})}$, ${(d,(e'_s)_{s\in S})}$ be diagonal pairs of $C$.
conclusions: Then $e_se'_s=e_s$ holds for $s\in S$.
nodes.label: different-projection

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5.4
nodes.statement_short: One-line computation inserting $d$ via the diagonal-pair axioms.

nodes.name: Heterogenization clone is independent of the idempotents
nodes.statement: Let $C$ be a $<\mathclose\kappa$-ary clone and ${(d,(e_s)_{s\in S})}$, ${(d,(e'_s)_{s\in S})}$ be diagonal pairs of $C$. Then $C_{(d,(e_s)_{s\in S})}$ is isomorphic to $C_{(d,(e'_s)_{s\in S})}$ via an isomorphism $\varphi=(\varphi_{(\lambda,v,s)})$ where \[ \varphi_{(\lambda,v,s)}:C_{(d,(e_s)_{s\in S}),(\lambda,v,s)}\ni f/\mathclose \sim\mapsto e'_sf(e_{v(i)}\pi_{(\lambda,i)})_{i\in\lambda}/\mathclose\sim' \in C_{(d,(e'_s)_{s\in S}),(\lambda,v,s)}. \] Here, $\sim$ and $\sim'$ are equivalences defined as \begin{align*} f\sim g:\Longleftrightarrow f\circ (e_{v(i)}\circ \pi_{(\lambda,i)})_{i\in\lambda} =g\circ (e_{v(i)}\circ \pi_{(\lambda,i)})_{i\in\lambda},\\ f\sim' g:\Longleftrightarrow f\circ (e'_{v(i)}\circ \pi_{(\lambda,i)})_{i\in\lambda} =g\circ (e'_{v(i)}\circ \pi_{(\lambda,i)})_{i\in\lambda}. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: For diagonal pairs with the same $d$, the heterogenization clones are isomorphic via an explicit map.
assumptions: Let $C$ be a $<\mathclose\kappa$-ary clone and ${(d,(e_s)_{s\in S})}$, ${(d,(e'_s)_{s\in S})}$ be diagonal pairs of $C$.
conclusions: Then $C_{(d,(e_s)_{s\in S})}$ is isomorphic to $C_{(d,(e'_s)_{s\in S})}$

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 5.5
nodes.statement: Well-definedness of $\varphi_{(\lambda,v,s)}$ directly follows from the definition. Let $\psi_{(\lambda,v,s)}:C_{(d,(e'_s)_{s\in S}),(\lambda,v,s)}\rightarrow C_{(d,(e_s)_{s\in S}),(\lambda,v,s)}$ be the mapping $g/\mathclose\sim'\mapsto e_sg(e'_{v(i)}\pi_{(\lambda,i)})_{i\in\lambda}/\mathclose\sim$. Then by the previous lemma, \begin{align*} \psi_{(\lambda,v,s)}\circ \varphi_{(\lambda,v,s)}(f/\mathclose\sim) =&\left(e_se'_sf(e_{v(i)}\pi_{(\lambda,i)})_{i\in\lambda} \circ(e'_{v(i)}\pi_{(\lambda,i)})_{i\in\lambda}\right)/\mathclose\sim\\ =&\left(e_sf(e_{v(i)}\pi_{(\lambda,i)})_{i\in\lambda}\right)/\mathclose\sim\\ =&f/\mathclose\sim. \end{align*} By the same way, $\varphi_{(\lambda,v,s)}\circ \psi_{(\lambda,v,s)}= \mathrm{id}_{C_{(d,(e'_s)_{s\in S}),(\lambda,v,s)}}$ holds. Thus $\psi_{(\lambda,v,s)}$ is the inverse of $\varphi_{(\lambda,v,s)}$. Particularly, $\varphi_{(\lambda,v,s)}$ is bijective. We prove $\varphi$ is compatible with $S$-sorted clone operations. Let $\pi_{(\lambda,v,i)}=e_{v(i)}\pi_{(\lambda,i)}/\mathclose\sim$ be the $(\lambda,v)$-ary $i$-th projection of $C_{(d,(e_s)_{s\in S})}$. Then \[ \varphi_{(\lambda,v,v(i))}(\pi_{(\lambda,v,i)}) =\left(e'_{v(i)}e_{v(i)}\pi_{(\lambda,i)}(e_{v(j)}\pi_{(\lambda,j)})_{j\in\lambda}\right)/\mathclose\sim' =(e'_{v(i)}e_{v(i)}\circ e_{v(i)}\pi_{(\lambda,i)})/\mathclose\sim' =e'_{v(i)}\pi_{(\lambda,i)}/\mathclose\sim' \] by the previous lemma. It is the $(\lambda,v)$-ary $i$-th projection of $C_{(d,(e_s)_{s\in S})}$. Next, let $\lambda_k<\kappa$, $v_k:\lambda_k\rightarrow S$ ($k=1,2$), $s\in S$ and \[ f/\mathclose\sim\in C_{(d,(e_s)_{s\in S}),(\lambda_1,v_1,s)}, g_i/\mathclose\sim\in C_{(d,(e_s)_{s\in S}),(\lambda_2,v_2,v_1(i))} \] for $i\in\lambda_1$. Then \begin{align*} &\varphi_{(\lambda_1,v_1,s)}(f/\mathclose\sim) \circ (\varphi_{(\lambda_2,v_2,v_1(i))}(g_i/\mathclose\sim))_{i\in\lambda_1}&\\ =&(e'_sf(e_{v_1(i)}\pi_{(\lambda_1,i)})_{i\in\lambda_1}/\mathclose\sim)\circ (e'_{v_1(i)}g_i(e_{v_2(j)}\pi_{(\lambda_2,j)})_{j\in\lambda_1}/\mathclose\sim)_{i\in\lambda_1}&\\ =&\left(e'_sf(e_{v_1(i)}e'_{v_1(i)}g_i)_{i\in\lambda_1}\circ (e_{v_2(j)}\pi_{(\lambda_2,j)})_{j\in\lambda_2}\right)/\mathclose\sim'&\\ =&\left(e'_sf(e_{v_1(i)}g_i)_{i\in\lambda_1}\circ (e_{v_2(j)}\pi_{(\lambda_2,j)})_{j\in\lambda_2}\right)/\mathclose\sim' &(\text{Lemma \ref{different-projection}})\\ =&\left(e'_sf(g_i)_{i\in\lambda_1}\circ (e_{v_2(j)}\pi_{(\lambda_2,j)})_{j\in\lambda_2}\right)/\mathclose\sim' &(g_i/\mathclose\sim\in C_{(d,(e_s)_{s\in S})})\\ =&\varphi_{(\lambda_2,v_2,s)}(f\circ (g_i)_{i\in\lambda_1}).& \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Exhibit an explicit inverse $\psi$ using Lemma 5.4, then check compatibility with projections and composition.

nodes.name: Heterogenized algebra is independent of the idempotents
nodes.statement: Let $C$ be a single-sorted $<\mathclose\kappa$-ary clone, ${(d,(e_s)_{s\in S})}$, ${(d,(e'_s)_{s\in S})}$ be diagonal pairs of $C$ and \mbox{$A=(A_s)_{s\in S}$} be a $C$-algebra. Then $A_{(d,(e_s)_{s\in S})}$ and $A_{(d,(e'_s)_{s\in S})}$ are isomorphic via $\varphi=(\varphi_t)_{t\in S}$ where \[ \varphi_s:A_{(d,(e_s)_{s\in S}),t}\ni a\mapsto e'_t(a)\in A_{(d,(e'_s)_{s\in S}),t}. \]
assumptions: Let $C$ be a single-sorted $<\mathclose\kappa$-ary clone, ${(d,(e_s)_{s\in S})}$, ${(d,(e'_s)_{s\in S})}$ be diagonal pairs of $C$ and \mbox{$A=(A_s)_{s\in S}$} be a $C$-algebra.
conclusions: Then $A_{(d,(e_s)_{s\in S})}$ and $A_{(d,(e'_s)_{s\in S})}$ are isomorphic

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 5.6
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{different-projection}, \[ a=e'_te_t(a), a'=e_te'_t(a') \] hold for $a\in A_{(d,(e_s)_{s\in S}),t}$ and $a'\in A_{(d,(e_s)_{s\in S}),t}$. Thus $a'\mapsto e_t(a')$ is the inverse of $\varphi_t$ and $\varphi_t$ is bijective. Let $f/\mathclose\sim\in C_{(d,(e_s)_{s\in S}),(\lambda,v,t)}$ and $a_i\in A_{(d,(e_s)_{s\in S}),v(i)}$. Then \begin{align*} \varphi_t((f/\mathclose\sim)(a_i)_{i\in \lambda}) &=e'_tf(a_i)_{i\in\lambda}\\ &=e'_tf(e_{v(i)}(a_i))_{i\in\lambda}\\ &=e'_tf(e_{v(i)}e'_{v(i)}(a_i))_{i\in\lambda}\\ &=e'_tf\circ(e_{v(i)}\pi_{(\lambda,i)})_{i\in\lambda}(e'_{v(i)}(a_i))_{i\in\lambda}\\ &=\varphi_{(\lambda,v,t)}(f/\mathclose\sim)(\varphi_{v(i)}(a_i))_{i\in\lambda}. \end{align*} This equation means $\varphi=(\varphi_t)_{t\in S}$ is a homomorphism $A_{(d,(e_s)_{s\in S})}$ to $A_{(d,(e'_s)_{s\in S})}$.
nodes.statement_short: By Lemma 5.4 the maps $e'_t$ and $e_t$ are mutually inverse; a computation shows they are homomorphisms.

nodes.name: Abbreviated heterogenization $C_d$
nodes.statement: In the following paragraph, we omit projection idempotents for writing heterogenization. Namely, we simply write $C_{d}$ the $S$-sorted clone $C_{(d,(e_s)_{s\in S})}$.

nodes.name: Heterogenization is a functor
nodes.statement: Let $C$ be a single-sorted $<\mathclose\kappa$-ary clone, $(d,(e_s)_{s\in S})$ be a diagonal pair of $C$, $\varphi:A\rightarrow B$ be a homomorphism of $C$-algebras. Then $\varphi_d:A_d\rightarrow B_d$ defined as $\varphi_{d,s}(a):=\varphi(a)$ for $s\in S,a\in A_{d,s}$ is a homomorphism of $C_d$-algebras. Further, the correspondence $d$ ($A\mapsto A_d$ for $A\in\mathcal{V}(C)$ and $\varphi\mapsto \varphi_d$ for morphisms of $C$-algebras) is a functor $\mathrm{Cat}(\mathcal{V}(C))\rightarrow \mathrm{Cat}(\mathcal{V}(C_d))$.
nodes.statement_short: Homomorphisms of $C$-algebras restrict to homomorphisms of heterogenized algebras, giving a functor $\mathrm{Cat}(\mathcal{V}(C))\to\mathrm{Cat}(\mathcal{V}(C_d))$.
assumptions: Let $C$ be a single-sorted $<\mathclose\kappa$-ary clone, $(d,(e_s)_{s\in S})$ be a diagonal pair of $C$, $\varphi:A\rightarrow B$ be a homomorphism of $C$-algebras.
conclusions: is a homomorphism of $C_d$-algebras.
is a functor $\mathrm{Cat}(\mathcal{V}(C))\rightarrow \mathrm{Cat}(\mathcal{V}(C_d))$.
nodes.label: single-many

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 5.7
nodes.statement: At first, notice that $a\in A_{d,s}=e_s(A)$ implies $\varphi(a)=\varphi(e_s(a))=e_s(\varphi(a))\in e_s(B)=B_s$. Thus $\varphi_{d,s}$ is actually a mapping $A_s\rightarrow B_s$. Let $f\in C_{d,(\lambda,v,s)}$, $a_i\in A_{d,v(i)}$. Then \begin{align*} \varphi_{d,s}((f/\mathclose\sim)(a_i)_{i\in\lambda}) &=\varphi f(a_i)_{i\in\lambda}\\ &=f(\varphi (a_i))_{i\in\lambda}\\ &=(f/\mathclose\sim)(\varphi_{d,v(i)} (a_i))_{i\in\lambda}. \end{align*} This equation means nothing but $\varphi_d$ is a homomorphism. It is easily verified that $d$ preserves identity and composition, thus $d$ is a functor.
nodes.statement_short: Check $\varphi$ maps $e_s(A)$ into $e_s(B)$ and commutes with term actions; functoriality is routine.

nodes.name: $({\rm H}(M))_d\cong M$
nodes.statement: Let $M$ be an $S$-sorted $<\mathclose\kappa$-ary pure clone. Let $d\in {\rm H}_S(M)$ and $e_s\in {\rm H}_1(M)$ ($s\in S$) be terms that satisfy the following properties: \begin{itemize} \item The term $d$ is defined as $d:=(\pi_{(S\times S,(s,s))})_{s\in S}$. \item Each $e_s$ can be written as in the form $e_s=(e_{s,t}\pi_{(S,\mathrm{id},s)})_{t\in S}$, where $e_{s,t}\in M_{s\rightarrow t}$ and satisfies \mbox{$e_{s,s}=\pi_{(\{s\},\mathrm{id},s)}$}. \end{itemize} Then $(d,(e_s)_{s\in S})$ is a diagonal pair of ${\rm H}(M)$ and $({\rm H}(M))_d$ is isomorphic to $M$ via an isomorphism \[ \mu_{(\lambda,v,s)}:M_{(\lambda,v,s)}\ni f \mapsto (e_{s,t})_{t\in S}\circ f\circ ( \pi_{(\lambda\times S,p_2,(i,v(i)))})_{i\in\lambda}/\mathclose\sim \in ({\rm H}(M))_{d,(\lambda,v,s)}, \] where $\sim$ is the equivalence \begin{align*} &(f_s)_{s\in S}\sim (g_s)_{s\in S}\\ :\Longleftrightarrow& (f_s)_{s\in S}\circ (e_{v(i)}\pi_{(\lambda,i)}^{{\rm H}(M)})_{i\in\lambda} =(g_s)_{s\in S}\circ (e_{v(i)}\pi_{(\lambda,i)}^{{\rm H}(M)})_{i\in\lambda}\\ \Longleftrightarrow& \forall s\in S; f_s\circ (e_{v(i),t}\pi_{(\lambda\times S,p_2,(i,v(i)))})_{(i,t)\in\lambda\times S} =g_s\circ (e_{v(i),t}\pi_{(\lambda\times S,p_2,(i,v(i)))})_{(i,t)\in\lambda\times S}, \end{align*} where $\pi^{{\rm H}(M)}$ denotes the projection constant of ${\rm H}(M)$.
nodes.statement_short: For a pure clone $M$, explicit $d,e_s$ form a diagonal pair of ${\rm H}(M)$ and the heterogenization $({\rm H}(M))_d$ is isomorphic to $M$ via $\mu$.
assumptions: Let $M$ be an $S$-sorted $<\mathclose\kappa$-ary pure clone.
conclusions: Then $(d,(e_s)_{s\in S})$ is a diagonal pair of ${\rm H}(M)$ and $({\rm H}(M))_d$ is isomorphic to $M$ via an isomorphism
nodes.label: clone-many

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 6.3
nodes.statement: First, we prove $(d,(e_s)_{s\in S})$ is a diagonal pair of ${\rm H}(M)$. 1. $e_s\circ d=e_s\circ \pi_{(S,s)}$ is proved as follows: \[ e_sd = e_s(\pi_{(S\times S,p_2,(t,t))}^M)_{t\in S} =e_s(\pi_{(S\times S,p_2,(s,t))}^M)_{t\in S} = e_s\circ \pi_{(S,s)}^{{\rm H}(M)}. \] Here and through the proof of this proposition, $\pi^M$ and $\pi^{{\rm H}(M)}$ denote projection constants of $M$ and ${\rm H}(M)$ respectively. 2. $d\circ(e_s\circ\pi_{(S,s)})=d$ is proved as follows: \begin{align*} d(e_s\circ \pi_{(S,s)}^{{\rm H}(M)})_{s\in S} &= (\pi_{(S\times S,p_2,(s,s))})_{s\in S} \circ (e_{s,t}\pi_{(S,\mathrm{id},s)}^M\circ (\pi_{(S\times S,p_2,(s,u))})_{u\in S})_{(s,t)\in S\times S}\\ &=(e_{s,s}\pi_{(S,\mathrm{id},s)}^M\circ (\pi_{(S\times S,p_2,(s,u))}^M)_{u\in S})_{s\in S} \\ &=(\pi_{(S\times S,p_2,(s,s))}^M)_{s\in S}\\ &=d. \end{align*} 3. $d\circ(\pi_{(S,0)})_{s\in S}=\pi_{(S,0)}$ is proved as follows: \begin{align*} d\circ (\pi_{(S,0)}^{{\rm H}(M)})_{s\in S} &=(\pi_{(S\times S,p_2,(s,s))}^M)_{s\in S} \circ (\pi_{(S\times S,p_2,(0,t))}^M)_{(s,t)\in S\times S}\\ &=(\pi_{(S\times S,p_2,(0,s))}^M)_{s\in S}\\ &=\pi_{(S,0)}^{{\rm H}(M)}. \end{align*} We complete the proof that $(d,(e_s)_{s\in S})$ is a diagonal pair of ${\rm H}(M)$. (Injectivity of $\mu_{(\lambda,v,s)}$) Let $f,g\in M_{(\lambda,v,s)}$ and assume $\mu_{(\lambda,v,s)}(f)=\mu_{(\lambda,v,s)}(g)$, namely, \begin{align*} &e_{s,t}f\circ(\pi_{(\lambda\times S,p_2,(i,v(i))}^M))_{i\in\lambda} \circ (e_{v(i),u}\pi_{(\lambda\times S,p_2,(i,v(i))})_{(i,u)\in\lambda\times S}\\ =&e_{s,t}g\circ(\pi_{(\lambda\times S,p_2,(i,v(i))}^M))_{i\in\lambda} \circ (e_{v(i),u}\pi_{(\lambda\times S,p_2,(i,v(i))})_{(i,u)\in\lambda\times S} \end{align*} hold for all $t\in S$. Notice that the following two equations hold: The first equation is \begin{align*} &\pi_{(\lambda,v,v(i))}^M\\ =&e_{v(i),v(i)}\circ \pi_{(\lambda,v,v(i))}^M \\ =&\pi_{(\lambda\times S,p_2,(i,v(i)))}^M \circ (e_{v(j),u}\circ \pi_{(\lambda,v,v(j))}^M)_{(j,u)\in\lambda\times S} \end{align*} The second equation is \[ \mathrm{id}_s:=\pi_{(\{s\},\mathrm{id}_{\{s\}},s)}^M=e_{s,s}\pi_{(S,\mathrm{id}_S,s)}^M (e_{s,t})_{t\in S}. \] By these equations injectivity of $\mu_{(\lambda,v,s)}$ is proved as follows: \begin{align*} f &=\mathrm{id}_s\circ f\circ (\pi_{(\lambda,v,v(i))}^M)_{i\in\lambda}\\ &=e_{s,s}\pi_{(S,\mathrm{id},s)}^M (e_{s,t})_{t\in S}\circ f (\pi_{(\lambda\times S,p_2,(i,v(i)))}^M)_{i\in\lambda} \circ (e_{v(j),u}\circ \pi_{(\lambda,v,v(j))}^M)_{(j,u)\in \lambda\times S}\\ &=e_{s,s}\pi_{(S,\mathrm{id},s)}^M (e_{s,t})_{t\in S}\circ g (\pi_{(\lambda\times S,p_2,(i,v(i)))}^M)_{i\in\lambda} \circ (e_{v(j),u}\circ \pi_{(\lambda,v,v(j))}^M)_{(j,u)\in \lambda\times S}\\ &=g. \end{align*} (Surjectivity of $\mu_{(\lambda,v,s)}$) Let $f/\mathclose\sim\in ({\rm H}(M))_{d,(\lambda,v,s)}$. Define $\tilde{f}$ by $\tilde{f}=\pi_{(S,\mathrm{id},s)}^M\circ f\circ (e_{v(i),u}\circ\pi_{(\lambda,v,i)})_{(i,u)\in \lambda\times S}$. Then the following formula holds. \begin{align*} \mu_{(\lambda,v,s)}(\tilde{f}) &=\left((e_{s,t})_{t\in S}\circ \tilde{f}\circ ( \pi_{(\lambda\times S,p_2,(i,v(i)))}^M)_{i\in\lambda}\right)/\mathclose\sim\\ &=\left((e_{s,t})_{t\in S}\circ \pi_{(S,\mathrm{id},s)}^M\circ f\circ (e_{v(i),u}\circ \pi_{(\lambda,v,i)}^M)_{(i,u)\in \lambda\times S}\circ (\pi_{(\lambda\times S,p_2,(i,v(i)))}^M)_{i\in\lambda}\right)/\mathclose\sim\\ &=\left(e_s\circ f\circ (e_{v(i),u}\circ \pi_{(\lambda,v,i)}^M)_{(i,u)\in \lambda\times S}\circ (\pi_{(\lambda\times S,p_2,(i,v(i)))}^M)_{i\in\lambda}\right)/\mathclose\sim\\ &=\left(f\circ (e_{v(i),u}\circ \pi_{(\lambda\times S,p_2,(i,v(i)))}^M)_{(i,u)\in\lambda\times S}\right)/\mathclose\sim\\ &= f/\mathclose\sim. \end{align*} (Compatibility of $\mu$) Let $f\in M_{(\lambda_1,v_1,s)}$ and $g_i\in M_{(\lambda_2,v_2,v_1(i))}$ for $i\in\lambda_1$. Then \begin{align*} &\mu_{(\lambda_2,v_2,s)}(f\circ (g_i)_{i\in\lambda_1})\\ =&\left((e_{s,t})_{t\in S}\circ f\circ (g_i)_{i\in\lambda_1} \circ (\pi_{(\lambda_2\times S,p_2,(j,v_2(j))}^M)_{j\in\lambda_2}\right)/\mathclose\sim\\ =&\left((e_{s,t})_{t\in S}\circ f\circ (e_{v_1(i),v_1(i)}g_i)_{i\in\lambda_1} \circ (\pi_{(\lambda_2\times S,p_2,(j,v_2(j))}^M)_{j\in\lambda_2}\right)/\mathclose\sim\\ =&\left((e_{s,t})_{t\in S}\circ f \circ (\pi_{(\lambda_1\times S,p_2,(i,v_1(i))}^M)_{i\in\lambda_1} \circ (e_{v_1(i),u})_{(i,u)\in\lambda_1\times S}\circ (g_i)_{i\in\lambda_1} \circ (\pi_{(\lambda_2\times S,p_2,(j,v_2(j))}^M)_{j\in\lambda_2}\right)/\mathclose\sim\\ =&\mu_{(\lambda_1,v_1,s)}(f)\circ (\mu_{(\lambda_2,v_2,v_1(i))}(g_i))_{i\in\lambda_1}. \end{align*} We complete the proof of the proposition.
nodes.statement_short: First verify the diagonal-pair identities, then prove $\mu$ injective, surjective (explicit preimage) and compatible with composition. Injectivity uses two identities expressing projections and $\mathrm{id}_s$ through $e_{s,t}$.

nodes.name: Natural isomorphism $A\cong({\rm H}(A))_d$
nodes.statement: Let $M,d,e_s,e_{s,t}$ be as in the previous proposition, $A=(A_s)_{s\in S}$ be an $M$-algebra. Then $({\rm H}(A))_d$ is isomorphic to $A$ via an isomorphism $\mu_A$, where \[ \mu_{A,s}:A_s\ni a\mapsto (e_{s,t}(a))_{t\in S}\in ({\rm H}(A))_{d,s}. \] Moreover, $(\mu_A)_{A\in\mathcal{V}(M)}$ is a natural transformation $\mathrm{id}_{\mathrm{Cat}(\mathcal{V}(M))}$ to $[A\mapsto ({\rm H}(A))_d]$.
nodes.statement_short: Every $M$-algebra is naturally isomorphic to the heterogenization of its homogenization via $a\mapsto(e_{s,t}(a))_t$.
assumptions: Let $M,d,e_s,e_{s,t}$ be as in the previous proposition, $A=(A_s)_{s\in S}$ be an $M$-algebra.
conclusions: Then $({\rm H}(A))_d$ is isomorphic to $A$ via an isomorphism $\mu_A$
$(\mu_A)_{A\in\mathcal{V}(M)}$ is a natural transformation $\mathrm{id}_{\mathrm{Cat}(\mathcal{V}(M))}$ to $[A\mapsto ({\rm H}(A))_d]$.
nodes.label: equiv-many

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 6.4
nodes.statement: Let $f\in M_{(\lambda,v,s)}$ and $a_i\in A_{v(i)}$ for $i\in\lambda$. Then \begin{align*} \mu_{(\lambda,v,s)}(f)(\mu_{A,v(i)}(a_i))_{i\in\lambda} &=(e_{s,t})_{t\in S}\circ f\circ (\pi_{(\lambda\times S,p_2,(i,v(i)))})_{i\in\lambda} (e_{v(i),u}(a_i))_{(i,u)\in\lambda\times S}\\ &=(e_{s,t})_{t\in S}\circ f(e_{v(i),v(i)}(a_i))_{i\in\lambda}\\ &=(e_{s,t})_{t\in S}\circ f(a_i)_{i\in\lambda}\\ &=\mu_{A,s}(f(a_i)_{i\in\lambda}). \end{align*} This equation is nothing but the proposition stated. We prove $(\mu_A)_{A\in\mathcal{V}(M)}$ is a natural transformation. Let $A=(A_s)_{s\in S},B=(B_s)_{s\in S}\in \mathcal{V}(M)$ and $\varphi=(\varphi_s)_{s\in S}$ be a homomorphism $A\rightarrow B$. We prove should the diagram \[\xymatrix{ A\ar[r]^{\mu_A} \ar[d]_\varphi& ({\rm H}(A))_d\ar[d]^{({\rm H}(\varphi))_d}\\ B\ar[r]^{\mu_B} & ({\rm H}(B))_d }\] commute. For $s\in S$ and $a\in A_s$, the equation \begin{align*} \mu_{B,s}(\varphi_s(a)) &=(e_{s,t}(\varphi_s(a))_{t\in S}\\ &=(\varphi_t(e_{s,t}(a)))_{t\in S}\\ &={\rm H}(\varphi)(e_{s,t}(a))_{t\in S}\\ &=({\rm H}(\varphi))_{d,s}(\mu_{A,s}(a)) \end{align*} holds. This is nothing but $\mu_B\circ \varphi=({\rm H}(\varphi))_d\circ \mu_A$, thus it is proved that $(\mu_A)_{A\in\mathcal{V}(M)}$ is a natural transformation.
nodes.statement_short: Compute that $\mu_A$ commutes with term actions using $e_{s,s}=\mathrm{id}$, then check the naturality square.

nodes.name: Argument for Theorems 6.5 and 6.6
nodes.statement: By Proposition \ref{clone-single} and \ref{clone-many}, there is natural correspondence between many-sorted pure clones and single-sorted clones with diagonal operations (that can be extended to diagonal pair). Proposition \ref{many-single},\ref{single-many},\ref{equiv-single} and \ref{equiv-many}, many-sorted varieties are essentially equivalent to single-sorted varieties that have diagonal pairs.
nodes.statement_short: Combine the clone isomorphisms (Props. 6.1, 6.3) with the functors and natural isomorphisms (Props. 3.5, 5.7, 6.2, 6.4).

nodes.name: Correspondence between pure many-sorted clones and clones with diagonal operations
nodes.statement: Let $\kappa$ be infinite cardinal and $S$ be a cardinal that $0<S<\kappa$. Then $(C,d)\mapsto C_d$ is one to one correspondence between (isomorphism classes of) single-sorted $<\mathclose\kappa$-ary clones with $S$-ary diagonal operations and (isomorphism classes of) $S$-sorted $<\mathclose\kappa$-ary pure clones. The converse correspondence is given by $M\mapsto ({\rm H}(M),(\pi_{(S\times S,p_2,(s,s))})_{s\in S})$.
nodes.statement_short: $(C,d)\mapsto C_d$ is a bijection between isomorphism classes of single-sorted clones with $S$-ary diagonal operations and $S$-sorted pure clones, inverse $M\mapsto({\rm H}(M),d)$.
assumptions: Let $\kappa$ be infinite cardinal and $S$ be a cardinal that $0<S<\kappa$.
conclusions: Then $(C,d)\mapsto C_d$ is one to one correspondence between (isomorphism classes of) single-sorted $<\mathclose\kappa$-ary clones with $S$-ary diagonal operations and (isomorphism classes of) $S$-sorted $<\mathclose\kappa$-ary pure clones.

nodes.name: Clone with an $S$-ary diagonal operation
nodes.statement: Here, a $<\mathclose\kappa$-ary clone with an $S$-ary diagonal operation means a tuple $(C,d)$ that $C$ is a $<\mathclose\kappa$-ary clone, $d\in C_S$ and there exists $(e_s)_{s\in S}$ such that $(d,(e_s)_{s\in S})$ is a diagonal pair of $C$.

nodes.name: Isomorphism of clones with diagonal operations
nodes.statement: Clones with diagonal operations $(C,d),(C',d')$ are said to be isomorphic if there is an clone isomorphism $\varphi:C\rightarrow C'$ such that $\varphi(d)=d'$.
differentia: there is an clone isomorphism $\varphi:C\rightarrow C'$ such that $\varphi(d)=d'$

nodes.name: Concrete categorical equivalence of many-sorted and single-sorted varieties
nodes.statement: Let $\kappa$ be infinite cardinal, $S$ be a cardinal that $0<S<\kappa$, $M$ be an $S$-sorted $<\mathclose\kappa$-ary clone. Then there exists a categorical equivalence $\nu:\mathcal{V}(M)\rightarrow \mathcal{V}({\rm H}(M))$ such that the following diagram commute. \[\xymatrix{ \mathcal{V}(M)\ar[r]^\nu \ar[d]_F& \mathcal{V}({\rm H}(M))\ar[d]^G\\ {\textbf{{\rm Set}}}^S \ar[r]^\varphi & {\cal D}_S }\] The vertical arrow $F$ is the forgetful functors attaining the underlying family of sets. $G$ is the forgetful functor determined by the clone homomorphism $d\in C_{{\cal D}_S}$ maps to $(\pi_{(S\times S,p_2,(s,s))}^M)_{s\in S}$. The lower horizontal arrow $\varphi$ is the functor described in Proposition \ref{pureset-and-sets}
nodes.statement_short: $\mathcal{V}(M)$ is categorically equivalent to $\mathcal{V}({\rm H}(M))$ compatibly with the forgetful functors and ${\textbf{{\rm Set}}}^S\simeq{\cal D}_S$.
assumptions: Let $\kappa$ be infinite cardinal, $S$ be a cardinal that $0<S<\kappa$, $M$ be an $S$-sorted $<\mathclose\kappa$-ary clone.
conclusions: Then there exists a categorical equivalence $\nu:\mathcal{V}(M)\rightarrow \mathcal{V}({\rm H}(M))$ such that the following diagram commute.
nodes.label: main-theorem-categorical-equivalence

nodes.name: Subalgebra and congruence of a many-sorted algebra
nodes.statement: Let $A=(A_s)_{s\in S}$ be an $S$-sorted algebra. \begin{enumerate} \item A subalgebra of $A$ is an $S$-sorted family $B=(B_s)_{s\in S}$ that satisfies the following conditions: \begin{itemize} \item $B_s\subset A_s$ for all $s\in S$. \item For $(\lambda,v)$-ary $s$-valued term operation $f$ of $A$ and $(b_i)_{i\in\lambda}\in \prod_{i\in\lambda}B_{v(i)}$, $f(b_i)_{i\in \lambda}\in B_s$ holds. \end{itemize} The set of all subalgebras of $A$ is denoted by $\mathrm{Sub}(A)$. \item A congruence of $A$ is a subalgebra $(\theta_s)_{s\in S}$ of $A^2=(A_s{}^2)_{s\in S}$ such that $\theta_s$ is an equivalence relation on $A_s$ for each $s\in S$. The set of all congruences of $A$ is denoted by $\mathrm{Con}(A)$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Sortwise subsets closed under term operations are subalgebras; congruences are sortwise equivalence relations forming a subalgebra of $A^2$.

nodes.name: Subalgebras and congruences under homogenization
nodes.statement: Let $M$ be an $S$-sorted clone, $A$ be an $M$-algebra. \begin{enumerate} \item If $B=(B_s)_{s\in S}\in \mathrm{Sub}(A)$, then ${\rm H}(B):=\prod_{s\in S}B_s\in \mathrm{Sub}({\rm H}(A))$. Conversely, Any subalgebra of ${\rm H}(A)$ is described as in the form ${\rm H}(B)$ by $B\in\mathrm{Sub}(A)$. \item If $\theta=(\theta_s)_{s\in S}\in\mathrm{Con}(A)$, then \[ {\rm H}(\theta):=\prod_{s\in S}\theta_s :=\{((a_s)_{s\in S},(b_s)_{s\in S})\in ({\rm H}(A))^2\mid \forall s\in S;(a_s,b_s)\in\theta_s\} \in\mathrm{Con}({\rm H}(A)). \] Conversely, Any congruence of ${\rm H}(A)$ is described as in the form ${\rm H}(\theta)$ by a congruence $\theta\in\mathrm{Con}(A)$. \item If $\theta\in \mathrm{Con}(A)$, then ${\rm H}(A/\theta){\simeq} {\rm H}(A)/{\rm H}(\theta)$. \item If $(A_i)_{i\in I}$ is a family of $M$-algebras, then \[ \prod_{i\in I}{\rm H}(A_i){\simeq} {\rm H}\left(\prod_{i\in I} A_i\right). \] \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Subalgebras, congruences, quotients and products of $M$-algebras correspond to those of their homogenizations.
assumptions: Let $M$ be an $S$-sorted clone, $A$ be an $M$-algebra.
conclusions: If $B=(B_s)_{s\in S}\in \mathrm{Sub}(A)$, then ${\rm H}(B):=\prod_{s\in S}B_s\in \mathrm{Sub}({\rm H}(A))$.
Conversely, Any subalgebra of ${\rm H}(A)$ is described as in the form ${\rm H}(B)$ by $B\in\mathrm{Sub}(A)$.
If $\theta\in \mathrm{Con}(A)$, then ${\rm H}(A/\theta){\simeq} {\rm H}(A)/{\rm H}(\theta)$.
nodes.label: sub-con-corresopndence

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 7.2
nodes.statement: We only show that any subalgebra of ${\rm H}(A)$ is in the form ${\rm H}(B)$ by a subalgebra $B$ of $A$. Other parts are easily verified or proved similarly. If ${\rm H}(A)= \emptyset$, then the assertion is trivial. Thus, we assume $A_s\neq\emptyset$ for all $s\in S$. Let $B'$ be a subalgebra of ${\rm H}(A)$. Define \[ B_s:=\{b\in A_s\mid\exists (a_t)_{t\in S\setminus\{s\}}\in\prod_{t\in S\setminus\{s\}}A_t; (b,(a_t)_{t\in S\setminus\{s\}})\in B'\}. \] Clearly, $B'\subset \prod_{s\in S}B_s$ holds. We show $\prod_{s\in S}B_s\subset B'$. Let $(b_s)_{s\in S}\in \prod_{s\in S}B_s$. By definition of $B_s$, there exist $(c_{st})_{t\in S}\in B'$ such that $c_{ss}=b_s$. Let $d=(\pi_{(S\times S,p_2,(s,s))})_{s\in S}$ be the diagonal term. Then \[ B'\ni d((c_{st})_{t\in s})_{s\in S}=(c_{ss})_{s\in S}=(b_s)_{s\in s}. \qedhere \]
nodes.statement_short: Only the subalgebra part is shown: project a subalgebra of ${\rm H}(A)$ to sorts and use the diagonal term to recover the full product.

nodes.name: Subalgebras of algebras over a pure clone
nodes.statement: If $M$ is a pure clone, then the underlying family of sets of any subalgebra of an $M$-algebra $A$ is pure. In such case, the correspondence $B\mapsto {\rm H}(B)$ between $\mathrm{Sub}(A)$ and $\mathrm{Sub}({\rm H}(A))$ is bijective. On the other hand, this correspondence may not be bijective if $M$ is not pure. For a simple example, $S=2=\{0,1\}$, $M$ be the trivial $2$-sorted clone (that is, the $2$-sorted clone only consists of projection constants) and $A=(A_i)_{i\in 2}=(A_0,A_1)$, then the both $(\emptyset,A_1)$ and $(A_0,\emptyset)$ of members of $\mathrm{Sub}(A)$ correspond to $\emptyset=\emptyset\times A_1=A_0\times\emptyset$.
nodes.statement_short: Over a pure clone, $B\mapsto{\rm H}(B)$ is a bijection $\mathrm{Sub}(A)\to\mathrm{Sub}({\rm H}(A))$; a trivial 2-sorted clone shows this fails without purity.
nodes.label: subalgebra-of-pure-algebra

nodes.name: Many-sorted Birkhoff variety theorem
nodes.statement: Let $M$ be an $S$-sorted pure clone, $\mathcal{K}$ be a class of $M$-algebras. Then the variety $\mathcal{V}(\mathcal{K})$ generated by $\mathcal{K}$ coincides with $\mathbf{HSP}(\mathcal{K})$.
assumptions: Let $M$ be an $S$-sorted pure clone, $\mathcal{K}$ be a class of $M$-algebras.
conclusions: Then the variety $\mathcal{V}(\mathcal{K})$ generated by $\mathcal{K}$ coincides with $\mathbf{HSP}(\mathcal{K})$.
nodes.label: variety-theorem

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 7.4
nodes.statement: We show \begin{equation} {\rm H}(\mathcal{V}(\mathcal{K}))=\mathcal{V}({\rm H}(\mathcal{K}))=\mathbf{HSP}({\rm H}(\mathcal{K}))={\rm H}(\mathbf{HSP}(\mathcal{K})). \end{equation} The second equality is Birkhoff's variety theorem for classes of single-sorted algebras. The last equality follows from Proposition \ref{sub-con-corresopndence}. The first equality is proved as follows. For $f,g\in {\rm H}_\lambda(M)$, where $f=(f_s)_{s\in S}$, $g=(g_s)_{s\in S}$, the following equivalence holds: \begin{align*} {\rm H}(\mathcal{V}(\mathcal{K}))\models f=g \Longleftrightarrow& \forall s\in S;\ \mathcal{V}(\mathcal{K})\models f_s=g_s\\ \Longleftrightarrow& \forall s\in S;\ \mathcal{K}\models f_s=g_s\\ \Longleftrightarrow& {\rm H}(\mathcal{K})\models f=g\\ \Longleftrightarrow& \mathcal{V}({\rm H}(\mathcal{K}))\models f=g. \end{align*} It means the equational theories defining $\mathcal{V}({\rm H}(\mathcal{K}))$ and ${\rm H}(\mathcal{V}(\mathcal{K}))$ coincide with each other. Therefore, ${\rm H}(\mathcal{V}(\mathcal{K}))=\mathcal{V}({\rm H}(\mathcal{K}))$ holds. By (\ref{varieties-through-homogenization}) and Theorem \ref{main-theorem-categorical-equivalence}, $\mathcal{V}(\mathcal{K})=\mathbf{HSP}(\mathcal{K})$ holds.
nodes.statement_short: Transfer through homogenization: show ${\rm H}(\mathcal{V}(\mathcal{K}))=\mathbf{HSP}({\rm H}(\mathcal{K}))={\rm H}(\mathbf{HSP}(\mathcal{K}))$ using single-sorted Birkhoff, then pull back by the categorical equivalence.

nodes.name: Varieties through homogenization
nodes.statement: {\rm H}(\mathcal{V}(\mathcal{K}))=\mathcal{V}({\rm H}(\mathcal{K}))=\mathbf{HSP}({\rm H}(\mathcal{K}))={\rm H}(\mathbf{HSP}(\mathcal{K})).
nodes.statement_short: Homogenization commutes with generating varieties and with $\mathbf{HSP}$.
nodes.label: varieties-through-homogenization

nodes.name: Clone-based variety theorem covers the type-based one
nodes.statement: As noted in preliminary section, the above clone-based formulation includes type-based formulation as the case that $M$ is a free clone. Thus, Theorem \ref{variety-theorem} above is essentially equivalent to usual formulation of variety theorem.

nodes.name: Denecke-Lüders theorem on categorical equivalence and relational clones
nodes.statement: Denecke and L\"{u}ders proved in \cite{DL} that two finite single-sorted algebras are categorically equivalent if and only if their relational clones are isomorphic.
assumptions: two finite single-sorted algebras
conclusions: are categorically equivalent if and only if their relational clones are isomorphic

nodes.name: Relational clone of a many-sorted algebra
nodes.statement: Let $A$ be an $S$-sorted $<\mathclose\kappa$-ary algebra, $\kappa'$ be a cardinal. A $<\mathclose\kappa'$-ary relational clone of $A$ is the family $\mathrm{Inv}_{<\mathclose\kappa'}(A)=(\mathrm{Inv}_\mu(A))_{\mu<\kappa'}$, where $\mathrm{Inv}_\mu(A)=\{{\rm H}(B)\mid B\in\mathrm{Sub}(A)\}$, namely, $\mathrm{Inv}_\mu(A)$ is the set of all subsets $r$ of $\left(\prod_{s\in S}A_s\right)^\mu$ that satisfy \begin{align*} &f_s\in \mathrm{Clo}_{(\lambda\times S,p_2,s)}(A),(a_{i,j,t})_{(t,j)\in S\times\mu}\in r\ (\text{for }i\in\lambda)\\ \Longrightarrow& (f_s(a_{i,j,t})_{(i,t)\in\lambda\times S})_{(s,j)\in S\times\mu}\in r. \end{align*} Here, $\mathrm{Clo}_{(\lambda,v,s)}(A)$ is the set of all $(\lambda,v)$-ary $s$-valued term operations of $A$. A member of $\mathrm{Inv}_\mu(A)$ is said an $\mu$-ary invariant set of $A$.
nodes.statement_short: $\mathrm{Inv}_\mu(A)$ consists of the $\mu$-ary relations on $\prod_s A_s$ closed under homogenized term operations ($\mu$-ary invariant sets).

nodes.name: Componentwise closed sets are not the right notion
nodes.statement: We can consider the set of all closed subsets for component-wise operations. Here, a set $r\subset \prod_{j\in\mu}A_{v(j)}$ ($\mu$ is a cardinal, $v:\mu\rightarrow S$) is said closed if the following condition holds: For $\mu<\kappa'$ and $v:\mu\rightarrow S$ \begin{align*} &f_j\in \mathrm{Clo}_{(\lambda,[i\mapsto v(j)],v(j))}(A),(a_{i,j})_{j\in\mu}\in r\ (\text{for }i\in\lambda)\\ \Longrightarrow& (f_j(a_{i,j})_{i\in\lambda})_{j\in\mu}\in r. \end{align*} However, this condition considers only on operations related at most one sort. Thus, it should be said a concept of the non-indexed product of an one-sorted algebras, rather than a concept of a many-sorted algebra.
nodes.statement_short: Sets closed only under sortwise term operations describe a non-indexed product of one-sorted algebras, not a many-sorted algebra.
