nodes.name: Relational clone of a many-sorted algebra equals that of its homogenization
nodes.statement: Let $M$ be an $S$-sorted $<\mathclose\kappa$-ary pure clone, $A$ be an $M$-algebra, and $\kappa'$ be an arbitrary cardinal. Then the $<\mathclose\kappa'$-ary relational clone $\mathrm{Inv}_{<\kappa'}(A)$ is isomorphic to $\mathrm{Inv}_{<\kappa'}({\rm H}(A))$.
assumptions: Let $M$ be an $S$-sorted $<\mathclose\kappa$-ary pure clone, $A$ be an $M$-algebra, and $\kappa'$ be an arbitrary cardinal.
conclusions: Then the $<\mathclose\kappa'$-ary relational clone $\mathrm{Inv}_{<\kappa'}(A)$ is isomorphic to $\mathrm{Inv}_{<\kappa'}({\rm H}(A))$.
nodes.label: many-single-relationa-clone

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 7.10
nodes.statement: By the definition of homogenization and relational clone, \[ \mathrm{Inv}_\mu(A)\ni r\mapsto \{((a_{j,s})_{s\in S})_{j\in\mu}\in ({\rm H}(A))^\mu\mid(a_{j,s})_{(j,s)\in\mu\times S}\in r\} \in \mathrm{Inv}_{\mu}({\rm H}(A)) \] is an isomorphism of relational clone. Note that the bijectivity of this correspondence follows from pureness of $M$ (Remark \ref{subalgebra-of-pure-algebra}).
nodes.statement_short: The obvious re-indexing map is an isomorphism; bijectivity uses purity (Remark 7.3).

nodes.name: Categorical equivalence of many-sorted algebras via relational clones
nodes.statement: Let $S_k$ be a non-zero cardinal, $\kappa$ be an infinite cardinal that $S_k<\kappa$ for $k=1,2$. Let $A_k$ be an $S_k$-sorted $<\mathclose\kappa$-ary algebra that the clones of term operations are pure for $k=1,2$. Let $\kappa'$ be an infinite cardinal that satisfies \[ \lambda<\kappa\ \Longrightarrow |A_1|^\lambda, |A_2|^\lambda <\kappa', \] where $|A_k|$ is the product cardinal $\prod_{s\in S_k} |A_{k,s}|$. Then the following assertions are equivalent. \begin{enumerate} \item There exists a categorical equivalence $\mathcal{V}(A_1)\rightarrow\mathcal{V}(A_2)$ that maps $A_1$ to $A_2$. \item The relational clones $\mathrm{Inv}_{<\mathclose\kappa'}(A_1)$ is isomorphic to $\mathrm{Inv}_{<\mathclose\kappa'}(A_2)$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: For many-sorted algebras with pure term clones, categorical equivalence mapping $A_1$ to $A_2$ holds iff their relational clones are isomorphic.
assumptions: Let $S_k$ be a non-zero cardinal, $\kappa$ be an infinite cardinal that $S_k<\kappa$ for $k=1,2$.
Let $A_k$ be an $S_k$-sorted $<\mathclose\kappa$-ary algebra that the clones of term operations are pure for $k=1,2$.
conclusions: There exists a categorical equivalence $\mathcal{V}(A_1)\rightarrow\mathcal{V}(A_2)$ that maps $A_1$ to $A_2$.
The relational clones $\mathrm{Inv}_{<\mathclose\kappa'}(A_1)$ is isomorphic to $\mathrm{Inv}_{<\mathclose\kappa'}(A_2)$.

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 7.11
nodes.statement: This corollary follows from Theorem \ref{main-theorem-categorical-equivalence}, Theorem \ref{many-single-relationa-clone} and the following theorem.
nodes.statement_short: Combine Theorem 6.6, Theorem 7.10 and the single-sorted Theorem 7.12.

nodes.name: Relational clone characterization of categorical equivalence (infinitary single-sorted)
nodes.statement: Let $\kappa$ be an infinite cardinal and $A_k$ be a single-sorted $<\mathclose\kappa$-ary algebra for $k=1,2$. Let $\kappa'$ be an infinite cardinal that satisfies $\lambda<\kappa\ \Longrightarrow |A_1|^\lambda,|A_2|^\lambda<\kappa'$. Then the following assertions are equivalent. \begin{enumerate} \item There exists a categorical equivalence $\mathcal{V}(A_1)\rightarrow\mathcal{V}(A_2)$ that maps $A_1$ to $A_2$. \item The relational clones $\mathrm{Inv}_{<\mathclose\kappa'}(A_1)$ is isomorphic to $\mathrm{Inv}_{<\mathclose\kappa'}(A_2)$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.origin_citation: Izawa, General theorems on category of infinitary algebras (in preparation)
assumptions: Let $\kappa$ be an infinite cardinal and $A_k$ be a single-sorted $<\mathclose\kappa$-ary algebra for $k=1,2$.
conclusions: There exists a categorical equivalence $\mathcal{V}(A_1)\rightarrow\mathcal{V}(A_2)$ that maps $A_1$ to $A_2$.
The relational clones $\mathrm{Inv}_{<\mathclose\kappa'}(A_1)$ is isomorphic to $\mathrm{Inv}_{<\mathclose\kappa'}(A_2)$.

nodes.name: Congruence permutability (many-sorted)
nodes.statement: Let $A$ be an $S$-sorted algebra. \begin{enumerate} \item Let $\theta_s,\eta_s\subset A_s{}^2$. A relational product $\theta\circ\eta$ of $\theta=(\theta_s)_{s\in S}$ and $\eta=(\eta_s)_{s\in S}$ is defined by sort-wise relational product $(\theta_s\circ\eta_s)_{s\in S}$. \item An algebra $A$ is said congruence permutable if $\theta\circ\eta=\eta\circ\theta$ for all $\theta,\eta\in\mathrm{Con}(A)$. \item A class of algebras $\mathcal{K}$ is said congruence permutable if all members of $\mathcal{K}$ are congruence permutable. \end{enumerate}

nodes.name: Many-sorted Mal'cev theorem
nodes.statement: Let $M$ be an $S$-sorted pure clone. Then the following conditions are equivalent. \begin{enumerate} \item $\mathcal{V}(M)$ is congruence permutable. \item $\mathcal{V}({\rm H}(M))$ is congruence permutable. \item There exists $p\in {\rm H}_3(M)$, called Mal'cev term, that satisfies \[ p(\pi_{(3,0)},\pi_{(3,0)},\pi_{(3,1)})=\pi_{(3,1)} ,p(\pi_{(3,0)},\pi_{(3,1)},\pi_{(3,1)})=\pi_{(3,0)}, \] where $3$ is a three elements set $\{0,1,2\}$. \item For each $s\in S$, there exists $p_s\in M_{(3\times S,p_2,s)}$ such that \begin{align*} p_s((\pi_{(3\times S,p_2,(0,t))})_{t\in S},(\pi_{(3\times S,p_2,(0,t))})_{t\in S},(\pi_{(3\times S,p_2,(1,t))})_{t\in S}) =\pi_{(3\times S,p_2,(1,t))},\\ p_s((\pi_{(3\times S,p_2,(0,t))})_{t\in S},(\pi_{(3\times S,p_2,(1,t))})_{t\in S},(\pi_{(3\times S,p_2,(1,t))})_{t\in S}) =\pi_{(3\times S,p_2,(0,t))}. \end{align*} \item For each $s\in S$, there exists $p_s\in M_{3s\rightarrow s}$ such that \begin{align*} p_s(\pi_{(3s\rightarrow s,0)},\pi_{(3s\rightarrow s,0)},\pi_{(3s\rightarrow s,1)}) =\pi_{(3s\rightarrow s,1)},\\ p_s(\pi_{(3s\rightarrow s,0)},\pi_{(3s\rightarrow s,1)},\pi_{(3s\rightarrow s,1)}) =\pi_{(3s\rightarrow s,0)}. \end{align*} \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: For a pure clone $M$, congruence permutability of $\mathcal{V}(M)$ is equivalent to that of $\mathcal{V}({\rm H}(M))$ and to existence of (sortwise) Mal'cev terms.
assumptions: Let $M$ be an $S$-sorted pure clone.
conclusions: $\mathcal{V}(M)$ is congruence permutable.
$\mathcal{V}({\rm H}(M))$ is congruence permutable.
nodes.label: malcev

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 7.14
nodes.statement: 1 $\Leftrightarrow$ 2 is an easy consequence of Proposition \ref{sub-con-corresopndence}. 2 $\Leftrightarrow$ 3 is well known Mal'cev's theorem (See e.g.{\cite[Theorem 12.2]{BS}}). 3 $\Leftrightarrow$ 4 follows from the definition of homogenization. 5 $\Rightarrow$ 4 is trivial. 1 $\Rightarrow$ 5. Let $F$ be a rank $(3\delta_{st})_{t\in S}$ free algebra, namely, there are three elements $a,b,c$ of sort $s$ such that $\{a,b,c\}$ freely generates $F$. Let $\theta$ and $\eta$ be congruences of $F$ generated by $(a,b)$ and $(b,c)$ respectively. Then $(a,c)\in\theta\circ\eta=\eta\circ\theta$, namely, there is $x\in F_s$ such that $(a,x)\in \eta$, $(x,c)\in\theta$. Let $p_s$ be the term corresponding to $x$, then equations stated in Condition 5 hold.
nodes.statement_short: Cycle of implications: transfer via Proposition 7.2, classical Mal'cev theorem, and a free-algebra argument for $1\Rightarrow5$.

nodes.name: Congruence permutability via idempotent retracts
nodes.statement: Let $C$ be a $<\mathclose\kappa$-ary single-sorted clone, $(d,(e_s)_{s\in S})$ be a diagonal pair of $C$. Then the following conditions are equivalent. \begin{enumerate} \item The variety $\mathcal{V}(C)$ is congruence permutable. \item The variety $\mathcal{V}(e_s(C))$ is congruence permutable for all $s\in S$. \end{enumerate}
assumptions: Let $C$ be a $<\mathclose\kappa$-ary single-sorted clone, $(d,(e_s)_{s\in S})$ be a diagonal pair of $C$.
conclusions: The variety $\mathcal{V}(C)$ is congruence permutable.
The variety $\mathcal{V}(e_s(C))$ is congruence permutable for all $s\in S$.

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 7.15
nodes.statement: Condition 1 of this corollary is equivalent to that $\mathcal{V}_d$ satisfy the condition 1 of the previous theorem. Condition 2 of this corollary is equivalent to that $\mathcal{V}_d$ satisfy the condition 5 of the previous theorem. Thus, these conditions are equivalent.
nodes.statement_short: Translate both conditions into conditions 1 and 5 of Theorem 7.14 for the heterogenization.

nodes.name: Limits of many-sorted Mal'cev conditions
nodes.statement: Similar results hold about congruence distributivity, modularity, etc.. However, many results on Mal'cev condition that does not fixed the number (or the form of equation) depend on finiteness of arity. In such case, the corresponding generalized results are limited. Moreover, we can construct some counter examples of infinitary or infinitely many-sorted classes by using the correspondence of many-sorted and single-sorted algebras.
nodes.statement_short: Analogues hold for distributivity and modularity, but Mal'cev conditions with unbounded terms depend on finitary arity, allowing infinitary counterexamples.

nodes.name: Many-sorted Jónsson theorem
nodes.statement: Let $S$ be a finite set, $M$ be an $S$-sorted finitary pure clone. Then the following conditions are equivalent: \begin{enumerate} \item $\mathcal{V}(M)$ is congruence distributive. \item $\mathcal{V}({\rm H}(M))$ is congruence distributive. \item There are an integer $n\geq 0$ and $d_0,\dots,d_{2n}\in {\rm H}_3(M)$, we call J\'onsson term of length $n$ in this paper, that satisfy the following equations: \begin{align*} d_0=\pi_{(3,0)},d_{2n}=\pi_{(3,2)}\\ d_{i-1}(\pi_{(3,0)},\pi_{(3,1)},\pi_{(3,0)})=d_{i}(\pi_{(3,0)},\pi_{(3,1)},\pi_{(3,0)}) &\ (1\leq i\leq 2n)\\ d_{2i}(\pi_{(3,0)},\pi_{(3,0)},\pi_{(3,2)})=d_{2i+1}(\pi_{(3,0)},\pi_{(3,0)},\pi_{(3,2)}) &\ (0\leq i\leq n-1)\\ d_{2i-1}(\pi_{(3,0)},\pi_{(3,2)},\pi_{(3,2)})=d_{2i}(\pi_{(3,0)},\pi_{(3,2)},\pi_{(3,2)}) &\ (1\leq i\leq n) \end{align*} \item There exists an integer $n\geq 0$ such that, for each $s\in S$, there exist $d_{s,i}\in M_{(3\times S,p_2,s)}$ ($0\leq i\leq 2n$) that satisfy the following equations: \begin{align*} &d_{s,0}=\pi_{(3\times S,p_2,(0,s))},d_{s,2n}=\pi_{(3\times S,p_2,(2,s))},&\\ &d_{s,i-1}((\pi_{(3\times S,p_2,(0,t))})_{t\in S},(\pi_{(3\times S,p_2,(1,t))})_{t\in S},(\pi_{(3\times S,p_2,(0,t))})_{t\in S})&\\ =&d_{s,i}((\pi_{(3\times S,p_2,(0,t))})_{t\in S},(\pi_{(3\times S,p_2,(1,t))})_{t\in S},(\pi_{(3\times S,p_2,(0,t))})_{t\in S}), &\ (1\leq i\leq 2n)\\ &d_{s,2i}((\pi_{(3\times S,p_2,(0,t))})_{t\in S},(\pi_{(3\times S,p_2,(0,t))})_{t\in S},(\pi_{(3\times S,p_2,(2,t))})_{t\in S})&\\ =&d_{s,2i+1}((\pi_{(3\times S,p_2,(0,t))})_{t\in S},(\pi_{(3\times S,p_2,(0,t))})_{t\in S},(\pi_{(3\times S,p_2,(2,t))})_{t\in S}), &\ (0\leq i\leq n-1)\\ &d_{s,2i-1}((\pi_{(3\times S,p_2,(0,t))})_{t\in S},(\pi_{(3\times S,p_2,(2,t))})_{t\in S},(\pi_{(3\times S,p_2,(2,t))})_{t\in S})&\\ =&d_{s,2i}((\pi_{(3\times S,p_2,(0,t))})_{t\in S},(\pi_{(3\times S,p_2,(2,t))})_{t\in S},(\pi_{(3\times S,p_2,(2,t))})_{t\in S}), &\ (1\leq i\leq n) \end{align*} \item For each $s\in S$, there exist an integer $n\geq 0$ and $d_{s,i}\in M_{(3\times S,p_2,s)}$ ($0\leq i\leq 2n$) that satisfy the same equations displayed in the previous condition. \item For each $s\in S$, there exist an integer $n\geq 0$ and $d_{s,i}\in M_{3s\rightarrow s}$ ($0\leq i\leq 2n$) that satisfy the following equations: \[ \begin{array}{cl} d_{s,0}=\pi_{(3s\rightarrow s,0)},d_{s,2n}=\pi_{(3s\rightarrow s,2)},&\\ d_{s,i-1}(\pi_{(3s\rightarrow s,0)},\pi_{(3s\rightarrow s,1)},\pi_{(3s\rightarrow s,0)}) =d_{s,i}(\pi_{(3s\rightarrow s,0)},\pi_{(3s\rightarrow s,1)},\pi_{(3s\rightarrow s,0)}), &(1\leq i\leq 2n)\\ d_{s,2i}(\pi_{(3s\rightarrow s,0)},\pi_{(3s\rightarrow s,0)},\pi_{(3s\rightarrow s,2)}) =d_{s,2i+1}(\pi_{(3s\rightarrow s,0)},\pi_{(3s\rightarrow s,0)},\pi_{(3s\rightarrow s,2)}), &(0\leq i\leq n-1)\\ d_{s,2i-1}(\pi_{(3s\rightarrow s,0)},\pi_{(3s\rightarrow s,2)},\pi_{(3s\rightarrow s,2)}) =d_{s,2i}(\pi_{(3s\rightarrow s,0)},\pi_{(3s\rightarrow s,2)},\pi_{(3s\rightarrow s,2)}). &(1\leq i\leq n) \end{array} \] \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: For a finite $S$ and finitary pure clone $M$, congruence distributivity of $\mathcal{V}(M)$ is equivalent to that of $\mathcal{V}({\rm H}(M))$ and to existence of (sortwise) Jónsson terms.
assumptions: Let $S$ be a finite set, $M$ be an $S$-sorted finitary pure clone.
conclusions: $\mathcal{V}(M)$ is congruence distributive.
$\mathcal{V}({\rm H}(M))$ is congruence distributive.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 7.16
nodes.statement: Equivalence of 1,2,3 and 4 is similar to corresponding equivalence of Theorem \ref{malcev}. 2 $\Leftrightarrow$ 3 is known as J\'onsson's theorem (See e.g. {\cite[Theorem 12.6]{BS}}). 5 $\Rightarrow$ 4 easily follows from finiteness of $S$. 6 $\Rightarrow$ 5 is trivial. 1 $\Rightarrow$ 6. Let $F$ be a rank $(3\delta_{st})_{t\in S}$ free algebra of $\mathcal{V}(M)$, $\{a,b,c\}$ be a set of free generators of $F$, and $\theta,\eta,\zeta$ be the congruences of $F$ generated by $(a,c),(a,b),(b,c)$ respectively. Then \[ (a,c)\in \theta\land(\eta\lor\zeta)=(\theta\land\eta)\lor(\theta\land\zeta). \] By finiteness of arity of $M$, the join in congruence lattice is described as $\alpha\lor\beta=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb{N}}(\alpha\circ\beta)^n$, where $(\alpha\circ\beta)^n$ denotes the $k$-th relational power of $\alpha\circ\beta$. Thus, there are $x_0,\dots,x_{2n}$ such that \[ x_0=a,x_{2n}=c,(x_{2i},x_{2i+1})\in\theta\land\eta, (x_{2i-1},x_{2i})\in\theta\land\zeta. \] The terms $d_{s,i}$ corresponding to $x_i$ satisfy the equations stated in Condition 6.
nodes.statement_short: As in Theorem 7.14: transfer via homogenization, Jónsson's theorem, and a free-algebra argument for $1\Rightarrow6$ using finitary joins.

nodes.name: Infinitary counterexample to Jónsson's theorem
nodes.statement: Let $S=\mathbb{N}=\aleph_0$ and $C_n$ be the $<\mathclose\aleph_1$-ary clone defined by the following presentation: \begin{itemize} \item The set of generators consists of 3-ary elements $d_0,\dots,d_{2n}$ and a nullary element $u$. \item The set of fundamental relations consists of J\'onsson equations, that is, equations displayed in Condition 3 of the previous theorem. \end{itemize} Let $C$ be the direct product clone $\prod_{n\in\mathbb{N}}C_n$ and define \[ d=(\pi_{(\aleph_0,i)})_{i\in\aleph_0}\in C_{\aleph_0}, e_n=(\pi_{(\{0\},0)},(u)_{i\in\aleph_0\setminus\{n\}})\in C_1 \] for $n\in\aleph_0$. (Intuitively, $d$ and $e_n$ are the operations such that $d:((a_{ij})_{j\in \mathbb{N}})_{i\in \mathbb{N}}\mapsto (a_{jj})_{j\in \mathbb{N}}$ and \mbox{$e_n:(a_i)_{i\in\mathbb{N}}\mapsto (a_n,(u)_{i\in\mathbb{N}\setminus\{n\}})$}.) Then $(d,(e_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}})$ is a diagonal pair of $C$. Moreover, the following assertions hold. \begin{enumerate} \item $\mathcal{V}(C)$ and $\mathcal{V}(C_d)$ are congruence distributive. \item $C$ does not have J\'onsson term. \item $C_d$ has terms that satisfy the equations stated in 6 of the previous theorem. \item $C_d$ is essentially finitary. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: A countably-sorted product of Jónsson-presented clones has a diagonal pair, is congruence distributive, yet lacks a Jónsson term while its heterogenization is essentially finitary.

nodes.name: Properties of the Jónsson counterexample
nodes.statement: Moreover, the following assertions hold. \begin{enumerate} \item $\mathcal{V}(C)$ and $\mathcal{V}(C_d)$ are congruence distributive. \item $C$ does not have J\'onsson term. \item $C_d$ has terms that satisfy the equations stated in 6 of the previous theorem. \item $C_d$ is essentially finitary. \end{enumerate}
conclusions: $\mathcal{V}(C)$ and $\mathcal{V}(C_d)$ are congruence distributive.
$C$ does not have J\'onsson term.
$C_d$ is essentially finitary.

nodes.name: Proof of Example 7.17
nodes.statement: 1. Each $C_n$ has J\'onsson term, thus $\mathcal{V}(C_n)$ is congruence distributive. Thus, \[ \mathcal{V}(C)=\mathcal{V}\left(\prod_{n\in\mathbb{N}}C_n\right){\simeq} \bigotimes_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\mathcal{V}(C_n) \] is congruence distributive. Here, $\otimes_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\mathcal{V}(C_n)$ denotes non-indexed product of the family $\{\mathcal{V}(C_n)\}_{n\in \mathbb{N}}$ of varieties. By Proposition \ref{sub-con-corresopndence}, $\mathcal{V}(C_d)$ also be congruence distributive. 2. If $C$ has J\'onsson term of length $n$, then $C_{n+1}$ also has J\'onsson term of length $n$. It is verified by the induction on $n$ that this is impossible. 3. It is easily verified that $e_n(C)$ is isomorphic to $C_n$. Particularly, $e_n(C)$ has J\'onsson term. These are nothing but the terms of $C_d$ satisfying Condition 6 of the theorem. 4. Let $f\in C_{d,(\aleph_0,v,n)}$, where $v:\aleph_0\rightarrow \mathbb{N}$ and $n\in\mathbb{N}$. By the definition of heterogenization, $f$ is represented by $\tilde{f}\in C_{\aleph_0}$ such that $e_n\circ\tilde{f}=\tilde{f}$. This condition implies that the $n$-th component of $\tilde{f}$ is an element of $C_n$ (it is finitary), and other components are $u$ (depend no variables). Therefore, $\tilde{f}$, particularly $f$, is finitary.
nodes.statement_short: Itemwise: products of congruence distributive varieties, an induction on $n$ for the missing Jónsson term, $e_n(C)\cong C_n$, and finitarity of representatives.

nodes.name: Homomorphism computation
nodes.statement: Let $f=(f_s)_{s\in S}\in {\rm H}_\lambda(M)$ and $a_i=(a_{i,s})_{s\in S}$ for $i\in\lambda$. Then \begin{align*} {\rm H}(\varphi)(f(a_i)_{i\in\lambda}) &={\rm H}(\varphi)(f_s(a_{i,t})_{(i,t)\in\lambda\times S})_{s\in S}\\ &=(\varphi_s f_s(a_{i,t})_{(i,t)\in\lambda\times S})_{s\in S}\\ &=(f_s(\varphi_t(a_{i,t}))_{(i,t)\in\lambda\times S})_{s\in S}\\ &=f({\rm H}(\varphi)(a_i))_{i\in\lambda}. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Compute that ${\rm H}(\varphi)$ commutes with homogenized operations.

nodes.name: Functoriality
nodes.statement: The correspondence ${\rm H}$ being a functor means \[ {\rm H}(\mathrm{id}_A)=\mathrm{id}_{{\rm H}(A)} \] holds for all $A\in\mathcal{V}(M)$, and \[ {\rm H}(\psi)\circ{\rm H}(\varphi)={\rm H}(\psi\circ\varphi) \] hold for all homomorphisms $\psi,\varphi$ that ${\rm cod}(\varphi)={\rm dom}(\psi)$. It is easily verified.
nodes.statement_short: Functor laws for ${\rm H}$ are routine.

nodes.name: Identity 1
nodes.statement: 1. \begin{align*} e_s\circ d =&e_s\circ (\pi_{(S\times S,p_2,(t,t))}^M)_{t\in S}&\\ =&e_s\circ (\pi_{(S\times S,p_2,(s,t))}^M)_{t\in S}&(e_s\text{ depends only on }s\text{-componet})\\ =&e_s\circ \pi_{(S,s)}^{{\rm H}(M)}.& \end{align*} Here and through the proof of this proposition, $\pi^M$ and $\pi^{{\rm H}(M)}$ denote projection constants of $M$ and ${\rm H}(M)$ respectively.
nodes.statement_short: Verify $e_s\circ d=e_s\circ\pi_{(S,s)}$.

nodes.name: Identity 2
nodes.statement: 2. \begin{align*} d\circ (e_s\circ \pi_{(S,s)}^{{\rm H}(M)})_{s\in S} =& (\pi_{(S\times S,p_2,(s,s))}^M)_{s\in S} \circ ((e_{s,t})_{t\in S}\circ (\pi_{(S\times S,p_2,(s,u))}^M)_{u\in S})_{s\in S}\\ =& (e_{s,s}\circ (\pi_{(S\times S,p_2,(s,u))}^M)_{u\in S})_{s\in S}\\ =& (\pi_{(S\times S,p_2,(s,s))}^M)_{s\in S}\\ =& d. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Verify $d\circ(e_s\pi_{(S,s)})_s=d$.

nodes.name: Identity 3
nodes.statement: 3. \begin{align*} d\circ (\pi_{(S,0)}^{{\rm H}(M)})_{s\in S} =&(\pi_{(S\times S,p_2,(s,s))}^M)_{s\in S} \circ (\pi_{(S\times S,p_2,(0,t))}^M)_{(s,t)\in S\times S}\\ =& (\pi_{(S\times S,p_2,(0,s))}^M)_{s\in S}\\ =& \pi_{(S,0)}^{{\rm H}(M)}. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Verify $d\circ(\pi_{(S,0)})_s=\pi_{(S,0)}$.

nodes.name: Homomorphism computation
nodes.statement: Let $f=(f_s\mathclose/\mathclose\sim_\lambda)_{s\in S}\in (\boxtimes_{s\in S}e_s(C))_{\lambda}$ and $a_{i}=(a_{i,s})_{s\in S}\in \boxtimes_{s\in S}e_s(A)$ for $i\in\lambda$. Then \begin{align*} \tilde{\varphi}(f(a_i)_{i\in\lambda}) &=(\varphi(f_s(a_{i,t})_{(i,t)\in\lambda\times S}))_{s\in S}\\ &=(f_s(\varphi(a_{i,t}))_{(i,t)\in\lambda\times S})_{s\in S}\\ &=f(\tilde{\varphi}(a_i))_{i\in\lambda}. \end{align*} The correspondence $\varphi\mapsto \tilde{\varphi}$ clearly preserves identity morphisms and composition.
nodes.statement_short: Compute that $\tilde\varphi$ commutes with the action; identities and composition are clearly preserved.

nodes.name: Functor
nodes.statement: Thus the correspondence is a functor.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude functoriality.

nodes.name: Membership and notation
nodes.statement: $d,\tilde{e}_s\in\boxtimes_{t\in S} e_t(C)$ immediately follows from the definition. In the proof of this proposition, we write $\pi^C$/$\pi^{\boxtimes e(C)}$ the projection terms of $C$/$\boxtimes_{s\in S}e_s(C)$ respectively.
nodes.statement_short: Note $d,\tilde e_s$ lie in the matrix product; fix projection notation.

nodes.name: Identity 1
nodes.statement: 1. \begin{align*} \tilde{e}_s\circ d =& \tilde{e}_s\circ (e_t\circ \pi_{(S\times S,(t,t))}^C)_{t\in S}&\\ =& \tilde{e}_s\circ (e_t\circ \pi_{(S\times S,(s,t))}^C)_{t\in S}& (\tilde{e}_s\text{ depends only on }s\text{-component})\\ =&\tilde{e}_s\circ \pi_{(S,s)}^{\boxtimes e(C)}.& \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Verify $\tilde e_s\circ d=\tilde e_s\circ\pi_{(S,s)}$.

nodes.name: Identity 2
nodes.statement: 2. \begin{align*} d\circ (\tilde{e}_s\circ \pi_{(S,s)}^{\boxtimes e(C)})_{s\in S} =& (e_t\circ \pi_{(S\times S,(t,t))}^C)_{t\in S} \circ ((e_t\pi_{(S,s)}^C)_{t\in S} \circ (\pi_{(S\times S,(s,t))}^C)_{t\in S})_{s\in S}\\ =& (e_t\circ \pi_{(S\times S,(t,t))}^C)_{t\in S} \circ ((e_t\pi_{(S\times S,(s,s))}^C)_{t\in S})_{s\in S}\\ =& (e_t\circ e_t\pi_{(S\times S,(t,t))}^C)_{t\in S}\\ =& (e_t\circ \pi_{(S\times S,(t,t))}^C)_{t\in S}\\ =& d. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Verify the second diagonal-pair identity using idempotency.

nodes.name: Identity 3
nodes.statement: 3. \begin{align*} d\circ (\pi_{(S,0)}^{\boxtimes e(C)})_{s\in S} =& (e_t\circ \pi_{(S\times S,(t,t))}^C)_{t\in S} \circ ((e_t\circ \pi_{(S\times S,(0,t))}^C)_{t\in S})_{s\in S}\\ =& (e_t\circ (e_t\circ \pi_{(S\times S,(0,t))}^C))_{t\in S}\\ =& (e_t\circ \pi_{(S\times S,(0,t))}^C)_{t\in S}\\ =& \pi_{(S,0)}^{\boxtimes e(C)}. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Verify the third diagonal-pair identity.

nodes.name: Define $\varphi_\lambda$
nodes.statement: Suppose $(d,(e_s)_{s\in S})$ is a diagonal pair of $C$. We define $\varphi_\lambda:C_\lambda\rightarrow (\boxtimes_{s\in S}e_s(C))_\lambda$ as \[ \varphi_\lambda:f\mapsto (e_s\circ f\circ (d\circ(\pi_{(\lambda\times S,(i,t))})_{t\in S}) _{i\in\lambda}/\mathclose\sim_\lambda)_{s\in \lambda}. \] Note that $\varphi_{\lambda}(f)\in (\boxtimes_{s\in S}e_s(C))_\lambda$ follows from $e_s\circ e_s=e_s$.
nodes.statement_short: Define $\varphi_\lambda$ and note it lands in the matrix product.

nodes.name: Injectivity
nodes.statement: We prove injectivity of $\varphi_\lambda$. Let $f,g\in C_\lambda$ and assume $\varphi_\lambda(f)=\varphi_\lambda(g)$, namely, assume the equality \begin{align*} &e_sf\circ(d\circ(e_t\pi_{(\lambda\times S,(i,t))})_{t\in S})_{i\in\lambda}\\ =&e_sf\circ (d\circ (\pi_{(\lambda\times S,(i,t))})_{t\in S})_{i\in\lambda} \circ (e_t\pi_{(\lambda\times S,(i,t))})_{(i,t)\in\lambda\times S}\\ =&e_sg\circ (d\circ (\pi_{(\lambda\times S,(i,t))})_{t\in S})_{i\in\lambda} \circ (e_t\pi_{(\lambda\times S,(i,t))})_{(i,t)\in\lambda\times S}\\ =&e_sg\circ(d\circ(e_t\pi_{(\lambda\times S,(i,t))})_{t\in S})_{i\in\lambda} \end{align*} hold for all $s\in S$. Then \begin{align*} f =&d\circ (e_s)_{s\in S}\circ f\circ (\pi_{(\lambda,i)})_{i\in\lambda}\\ =&d\circ (e_s)_{s\in S}\circ f\circ (d\circ (\pi_{(\lambda,i)})_{t\in S})_{i\in\lambda}\\ =&d\circ (e_s)_{s\in S}\circ f\circ (d\circ (\pi_{(\lambda\times S,(i,t))})_{t\in S})_{i\in\lambda} \circ (\pi_{(\lambda,i)})_{(i,t)\in\lambda\times S}\\ =&d\circ (e_s)_{s\in S}\circ f\circ (d\circ (e_t\pi_{(\lambda\times S,(i,t))})_{t\in S})_{i\in\lambda} \circ (\pi_{(\lambda,i)})_{(i,t)\in\lambda\times S}\\ =&d\circ (e_s)_{s\in S}\circ g\circ (d\circ (e_t\pi_{(\lambda\times S,(i,t))})_{t\in S})_{i\in\lambda} \circ (\pi_{(\lambda,i)})_{(i,t)\in\lambda\times S}\\ =&g. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Recover $f$ from $\varphi_\lambda(f)$ using the diagonal-pair identities.

nodes.name: Surjectivity
nodes.statement: Next, we prove surjectivity of $\varphi_\lambda$. Let $(f_s\mathclose/\mathclose\sim_{\lambda})_{s\in S}\in(\boxtimes_{s\in S}e_s(C))_\lambda$. We define $\tilde{f}\in C_\lambda$ as \[ \tilde{f}:=d\circ (f_s)_{s\in S}\circ (e_t\pi_{(\lambda,i)})_{(i,t)\in\lambda\times S}. \] Then \begin{align*} \varphi_{\lambda}(\tilde{f}) =&\left(e_sd\circ (f_t)_{t\in S} \circ (e_t\pi_{(\lambda,i)})_{(i,t)\in\lambda\times S} \circ (d\circ (\pi_{(\lambda\times S,(i,u))})_{u\in S})_{i\in\lambda}\mathclose/\mathclose\sim_{\lambda}\right)_{s\in S}\\ =&\left(e_sf_s \circ (e_td\circ (\pi_{(\lambda\times S,(i,u))})_{u\in S})_{(i,t)\in\lambda\times S}\mathclose/\mathclose\sim_{\lambda}\right)_{s\in S}\\ =&\left(f_s \circ (e_t\pi_{(\lambda\times S,(i,t))})_{(i,t)\in\lambda\times S}\mathclose/\mathclose\sim_{\lambda}\right)_{s\in S}\\ =&(f_s\mathclose/\mathclose\sim_{\lambda})_{s\in S}. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Construct an explicit preimage $\tilde f$.

nodes.name: Define preimage
nodes.statement: Let $(f_s\mathclose/\mathclose\sim_{\lambda})_{s\in S}\in(\boxtimes_{s\in S}e_s(C))_\lambda$. We define $\tilde{f}\in C_\lambda$ as \[ \tilde{f}:=d\circ (f_s)_{s\in S}\circ (e_t\pi_{(\lambda,i)})_{(i,t)\in\lambda\times S}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Define $\tilde f=d\circ(f_s)\circ(e_t\pi_{(\lambda,i)})$.

nodes.name: Check preimage
nodes.statement: Then \begin{align*} \varphi_{\lambda}(\tilde{f}) =&\left(e_sd\circ (f_t)_{t\in S} \circ (e_t\pi_{(\lambda,i)})_{(i,t)\in\lambda\times S} \circ (d\circ (\pi_{(\lambda\times S,(i,u))})_{u\in S})_{i\in\lambda}\mathclose/\mathclose\sim_{\lambda}\right)_{s\in S}\\ =&\left(e_sf_s \circ (e_td\circ (\pi_{(\lambda\times S,(i,u))})_{u\in S})_{(i,t)\in\lambda\times S}\mathclose/\mathclose\sim_{\lambda}\right)_{s\in S}\\ =&\left(f_s \circ (e_t\pi_{(\lambda\times S,(i,t))})_{(i,t)\in\lambda\times S}\mathclose/\mathclose\sim_{\lambda}\right)_{s\in S}\\ =&(f_s\mathclose/\mathclose\sim_{\lambda})_{s\in S}. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Compute $\varphi_\lambda(\tilde f)=(f_s/\sim)_s$.

nodes.name: Homomorphism
nodes.statement: Finally, we prove $\varphi=(\varphi_{\lambda})_{\lambda<\kappa}$ is a homomorphism. Let $\lambda_1,\lambda_2<\kappa$ and $f\in C_{\lambda_1}$, $g_i\in C_{\lambda_2}$ for $i\in\lambda_1$. Then \begin{align*} &\varphi_{\lambda_2}(f\circ (g_i)_{i\in\lambda_1})\\ =&\left(e_s f\circ (g_i)_{i\in\lambda_1} \circ (d\circ (\pi_{(\lambda_2\times S,(j,t))})_{t\in S})_{j\in\lambda_2}\mathclose/\mathclose\sim_{\lambda_2}\right)_{s\in S}\\ =&\left(e_sf\circ (d\circ (g_i)_{u\in S})_{i\in\lambda_1} \circ (d\circ (\pi_{(\lambda_2\times S,(j,t))})_{t\in S})_{j\in\lambda_2}\mathclose/\mathclose\sim_{\lambda_2}\right)_{s\in S}\\ =&\left(e_s f\circ (d\circ (e_ug_i)_{u\in S})_{i\in\lambda_1} \circ (d\circ (\pi_{(\lambda_2\times S,(j,t))})_{t\in S})_{j\in\lambda_2}\mathclose/\mathclose\sim_{\lambda_2}\right)_{s\in S}\\ =&\left(e_s f\circ (d\circ (\pi_{(\lambda_1\times S,(i,u))})_{u\in S})_{i\in\lambda_1} \circ (e_ug_i)_{(i,u)\in\lambda_1\times S} \circ (d\circ (\pi_{(\lambda_2\times S,(j,t))})_{t\in S})_{j\in\lambda_2}\mathclose/\mathclose\sim_{\lambda_2}\right)_{s\in S}\\ =&\left(e_s f\circ (d\circ (\pi_{(\lambda_1\times S,(i,u))})_{u\in S})_{i\in\lambda_1}\mathclose/\mathclose\sim_{\lambda_1}\right)_{s\in S} \circ \left(e_ug_i \circ (d\circ (\pi_{(\lambda_2\times S,(j,t))})_{t\in S})_{j\in\lambda_2}\mathclose/\mathclose\sim_{\lambda_2}\right)_{(i,u)\in \lambda_1\times S}\\ =&\varphi_{\lambda_1}(f)\circ (\varphi_{\lambda_2}(g_i))_{i\in\lambda_1}. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Show $\varphi$ preserves composition.

nodes.name: Well-definedness
nodes.statement: Well-definedness of $\varphi_{(\lambda,v,s)}$ directly follows from the definition.
nodes.statement_short: Well-definedness is immediate.

nodes.name: Bijectivity
nodes.statement: Let $\psi_{(\lambda,v,s)}:C_{(d,(e'_s)_{s\in S}),(\lambda,v,s)}\rightarrow C_{(d,(e_s)_{s\in S}),(\lambda,v,s)}$ be the mapping $g/\mathclose\sim'\mapsto e_sg(e'_{v(i)}\pi_{(\lambda,i)})_{i\in\lambda}/\mathclose\sim$. Then by the previous lemma, \begin{align*} \psi_{(\lambda,v,s)}\circ \varphi_{(\lambda,v,s)}(f/\mathclose\sim) =&\left(e_se'_sf(e_{v(i)}\pi_{(\lambda,i)})_{i\in\lambda} \circ(e'_{v(i)}\pi_{(\lambda,i)})_{i\in\lambda}\right)/\mathclose\sim\\ =&\left(e_sf(e_{v(i)}\pi_{(\lambda,i)})_{i\in\lambda}\right)/\mathclose\sim\\ =&f/\mathclose\sim. \end{align*} By the same way, $\varphi_{(\lambda,v,s)}\circ \psi_{(\lambda,v,s)}= \mathrm{id}_{C_{(d,(e'_s)_{s\in S}),(\lambda,v,s)}}$ holds. Thus $\psi_{(\lambda,v,s)}$ is the inverse of $\varphi_{(\lambda,v,s)}$. Particularly, $\varphi_{(\lambda,v,s)}$ is bijective.
nodes.statement_short: Show the map $\psi$ is an inverse using Lemma 5.4.

nodes.name: Projections preserved
nodes.statement: We prove $\varphi$ is compatible with $S$-sorted clone operations. Let $\pi_{(\lambda,v,i)}=e_{v(i)}\pi_{(\lambda,i)}/\mathclose\sim$ be the $(\lambda,v)$-ary $i$-th projection of $C_{(d,(e_s)_{s\in S})}$.
nodes.statement_short: Check $\varphi$ maps projections to projections.

nodes.name: Composition preserved
nodes.statement: Next, let $\lambda_k<\kappa$, $v_k:\lambda_k\rightarrow S$ ($k=1,2$), $s\in S$ and \[ f/\mathclose\sim\in C_{(d,(e_s)_{s\in S}),(\lambda_1,v_1,s)}, g_i/\mathclose\sim\in C_{(d,(e_s)_{s\in S}),(\lambda_2,v_2,v_1(i))} \] for $i\in\lambda_1$. Then \begin{align*} &\varphi_{(\lambda_1,v_1,s)}(f/\mathclose\sim) \circ (\varphi_{(\lambda_2,v_2,v_1(i))}(g_i/\mathclose\sim))_{i\in\lambda_1}&\\ =&(e'_sf(e_{v_1(i)}\pi_{(\lambda_1,i)})_{i\in\lambda_1}/\mathclose\sim)\circ (e'_{v_1(i)}g_i(e_{v_2(j)}\pi_{(\lambda_2,j)})_{j\in\lambda_1}/\mathclose\sim)_{i\in\lambda_1}&\\ =&\left(e'_sf(e_{v_1(i)}e'_{v_1(i)}g_i)_{i\in\lambda_1}\circ (e_{v_2(j)}\pi_{(\lambda_2,j)})_{j\in\lambda_2}\right)/\mathclose\sim'&\\ =&\left(e'_sf(e_{v_1(i)}g_i)_{i\in\lambda_1}\circ (e_{v_2(j)}\pi_{(\lambda_2,j)})_{j\in\lambda_2}\right)/\mathclose\sim' &(\text{Lemma \ref{different-projection}})\\ =&\left(e'_sf(g_i)_{i\in\lambda_1}\circ (e_{v_2(j)}\pi_{(\lambda_2,j)})_{j\in\lambda_2}\right)/\mathclose\sim' &(g_i/\mathclose\sim\in C_{(d,(e_s)_{s\in S})})\\ =&\varphi_{(\lambda_2,v_2,s)}(f\circ (g_i)_{i\in\lambda_1}).& \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Check $\varphi$ preserves composition.

nodes.name: Bijectivity
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{different-projection}, \[ a=e'_te_t(a), a'=e_te'_t(a') \] hold for $a\in A_{(d,(e_s)_{s\in S}),t}$ and $a'\in A_{(d,(e_s)_{s\in S}),t}$. Thus $a'\mapsto e_t(a')$ is the inverse of $\varphi_t$ and $\varphi_t$ is bijective.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 5.4 gives mutually inverse maps.

nodes.name: Homomorphism
nodes.statement: Let $f/\mathclose\sim\in C_{(d,(e_s)_{s\in S}),(\lambda,v,t)}$ and $a_i\in A_{(d,(e_s)_{s\in S}),v(i)}$. Then \begin{align*} \varphi_t((f/\mathclose\sim)(a_i)_{i\in \lambda}) &=e'_tf(a_i)_{i\in\lambda}\\ &=e'_tf(e_{v(i)}(a_i))_{i\in\lambda}\\ &=e'_tf(e_{v(i)}e'_{v(i)}(a_i))_{i\in\lambda}\\ &=e'_tf\circ(e_{v(i)}\pi_{(\lambda,i)})_{i\in\lambda}(e'_{v(i)}(a_i))_{i\in\lambda}\\ &=\varphi_{(\lambda,v,t)}(f/\mathclose\sim)(\varphi_{v(i)}(a_i))_{i\in\lambda}. \end{align*} This equation means $\varphi=(\varphi_t)_{t\in S}$ is a homomorphism $A_{(d,(e_s)_{s\in S})}$ to $A_{(d,(e'_s)_{s\in S})}$.
nodes.statement_short: Compute that $\varphi$ commutes with term actions.

nodes.name: Well-defined on sorts
nodes.statement: At first, notice that $a\in A_{d,s}=e_s(A)$ implies $\varphi(a)=\varphi(e_s(a))=e_s(\varphi(a))\in e_s(B)=B_s$. Thus $\varphi_{d,s}$ is actually a mapping $A_s\rightarrow B_s$.
nodes.statement_short: $\varphi$ maps $e_s(A)$ into $e_s(B)$.

nodes.name: Homomorphism and functoriality
nodes.statement: Let $f\in C_{d,(\lambda,v,s)}$, $a_i\in A_{d,v(i)}$. Then \begin{align*} \varphi_{d,s}((f/\mathclose\sim)(a_i)_{i\in\lambda}) &=\varphi f(a_i)_{i\in\lambda}\\ &=f(\varphi (a_i))_{i\in\lambda}\\ &=(f/\mathclose\sim)(\varphi_{d,v(i)} (a_i))_{i\in\lambda}. \end{align*} This equation means nothing but $\varphi_d$ is a homomorphism. It is easily verified that $d$ preserves identity and composition, thus $d$ is a functor.
nodes.statement_short: $\varphi_d$ commutes with term actions; functor laws are routine.

nodes.name: (Injectivity)
nodes.statement:
(Injectivity) Let $f,g\in C_\lambda$ and assume $
u_\lambda(f)=
u_\lambda(g)$, namely  egin{align*} &e_sf\circ (d\circ (\pi_{(\lambda	imes S,(i,t))})_{t\in S})_{i\in\lambda} \circ (e_t\circ \pi_{(\lambda	imes S,(i,t))})_{(i,t)\in\lambda	imes S}\ =&e_sg\circ (d\circ (\pi_{(\lambda	imes S,(i,t))})_{t\in S})_{i\in\lambda} \circ (e_t\circ \pi_{(\lambda	imes S,(i,t))})_{(i,t)\in\lambda	imes S} \end{align*} holds for all $s\in S$. Then  egin{align*} f &=d\circ (e_sf)_{s\in S}\ &=d\circ (e_sf)_{s\in S}\circ (\pi_{(\lambda,i)})_{i\in\lambda}\ &=d\circ (e_sf)_{s\in S}\circ (d\circ (\pi_{(\lambda,i)})_{t\in S})_{i\in\lambda}\ &=d\circ (e_sf)_{s\in S}\circ (d\circ (\pi_{(\lambda	imes S,(i,t))})_{t\in S})_{i\in\lambda} \circ (\pi_{(\lambda,i)})_{(i,t)\in\lambda	imes S}\ &=d\circ (e_sf)_{s\in S}\circ (d\circ (e_t\pi_{(\lambda	imes S,(i,t))})_{t\in S})_{i\in\lambda} \circ (\pi_{(\lambda,i)})_{(i,t)\in\lambda	imes S}\ &=d\circ (e_sf)_{s\in S}\circ (d\circ (\pi_{(\lambda	imes S,(i,t))})_{t\in S})_{i\in\lambda} \circ (e_t\pi_{(\lambda	imes S,(i,t))})_{(i,t)\in\lambda}\circ (\pi_{(\lambda,i)})_{(i,t)\in\lambda	imes S}\ &=d\circ (e_sg)_{s\in S}\circ (d\circ (\pi_{(\lambda	imes S,(i,t))})_{t\in S})_{i\in\lambda} \circ (e_t\pi_{(\lambda	imes S,(i,t))})_{(i,t)\in\lambda}\circ (\pi_{(\lambda,i)})_{(i,t)\in\lambda	imes S}\ &=g. \end{align*} Thus, $
u_\lambda$ is injective.
nodes.statement_short: Recover $f$ from $\nu_\lambda(f)$ via the diagonal-pair identities.

nodes.name: (Surjectivity)
nodes.statement: (Surjectivity) Suppose $f\in {\rm H}(C_d)$. By definition of ${\rm H}(C_d)$, $f$ is described as $f=(f_s/\mathclose\sim)_{s\in S}$ where $f_s\in C_{\lambda\times S}$ and each $f_s$ satisfies $e_sf_s=f_s$. Let us define \[ \tilde{f}:=d\circ (f_s)_{s\in S} \circ(e_t\pi_{(\lambda,i)})_{(i,t)\in\lambda\times S}. \] Then $\nu_\lambda(\tilde{f})$ is calculated as follows: \begin{align*} \nu_\lambda(\tilde{f}) &= \left(e_s\tilde{f} \circ (d\circ (\pi_{(\lambda\times S,(i,u))})_{u\in S})_{i\in\lambda}/\sim\right)_{s\in S}\\ &=\left(e_s d\circ (f_{s'})_{s'\in S} \circ(e_t\pi_{(\lambda,i)})_{(i,t)\in\lambda\times S} \circ (d\circ (\pi_{(\lambda\times S,(i,u))})_{u\in S})_{i\in\lambda}/\mathclose\sim\right)_{s\in S}\\ &=\left(f_{s} \circ (e_t\circ \pi_{(\lambda,i)})_{(i,t)\in\lambda\times S} \circ (d\circ (\pi_{(\lambda\times S,(i,u))})_{u\in S})_{i\in\lambda}/\mathclose\sim\right)_{s\in S}\\ &=\left(f_{s} \circ (e_td\circ (\pi_{(\lambda\times S,(i,u))})_{u\in S})_{(i,t)\in\lambda\times S}/\sim\right)_{s\in S}\\ &=\left(f_{s} \circ (e_t\pi_{(\lambda\times S,(i,t))})_{(i,t)\in\lambda\times S}/\mathclose\sim\right)_{s\in S}\\ &=(f_{s}/\mathclose\sim)_{s\in S}\\ &=f. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Explicit preimage $\tilde f$.

nodes.name: (Compatibility)
nodes.statement:
(Compatibility) Let $f\in C_{\lambda_1}$, $g_i\in C_{\lambda_2}$ ($i\in \lambda_1$). Then  egin{align*} &
u_{\lambda_2}(f\circ (g_i)_{i\in\lambda_1})\ =&\left(e_s f\circ(g_i)_{i\in\lambda_1} \circ(d\circ(\pi_{(\lambda_2	imes S,(j,t))})_{t\in S})_{j\in\lambda_2}/\mathclose\simight)_{s\in S}\ =&\left(e_s f \circ (d\circ(e_u\circ \pi_{(\lambda_1,i)})_{u\in S})_{i\in\lambda_1} \circ(g_i)_{i\in\lambda_1} \circ(d\circ(\pi_{(\lambda_2	imes S,(j,t))})_{t\in S})_{j\in\lambda_2}/\mathclose\simight)_{s\in S}\ =&\left(e_s f \circ (d\circ(\pi_{(\lambda_1	imes S,(i,u))})_{u\in S})_{i\in\lambda_1} \circ(e_u g_i)_{(i,u)\in\lambda_1	imes S} \circ(d\circ(\pi_{(\lambda_2	imes S,(j,t))})_{t\in S})_{j\in\lambda_2}/\mathclose\simight)_{s\in S}\ =&
u_{\lambda_1}(f)\circ (
u_{\lambda_2}(g_i))_{i\in\lambda_1}. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: $\nu$ preserves composition.

nodes.name: Bijectivity
nodes.statement: By definition of diagonal pair, $(a_s)_{s\in S}\mapsto d(a_s)_{s\in S}$ is the inverse mapping of $\nu_A$. Thus $\nu_A$ is bijective.
nodes.statement_short: $d$ gives the inverse of $\nu_A$.

nodes.name: Homomorphism
nodes.statement:
We prove $
u_A$ is a homomorphism of $C$-algebras. Let $f\in C_\lambda$, $\lambda<\kappa$ and $(a_i)_{i\in\lambda}\in A^\lambda$. Then  egin{align*} 
u_\lambda(f)(
u_A(a_i))_{i\in\lambda} &=(e_sf(d(e_t(a_i))_{t\in S})_{i\in\lambda})_{s\in S}\ &=(e_sf(a_i)_{i\in\lambda})_{s\in S}\ &=
u_A(f(a_i)_{i\in\lambda}). \end{align*} This equation is nothing but the property we should prove.
nodes.statement_short: Compute that $\nu_A$ commutes with term actions.

nodes.name: Naturality
nodes.statement:
Next, we prove naturalness of $(
u_A)_{A\in\mathcal{V}(C)}$. Let $A,B\in\mathcal{V}(C)$ and $\varphi:Aightarrow B$ be a homomorphism. We should the diagram \[\xymatrix{ A\ar[r]^{
u_A} \ar[d]_\varphi& {m H}(A_d)\ar[d]^{{m H}(\varphi_d)}\ B\ar[r]^{
u_B} & {m H}(B_d) }\] commute. For $a\in A$,  egin{align*} {m H}(\varphi_d)(
u_A(a)) &={m H}(\varphi_d)(e_s(a))_{s\in S}\ &=(\varphi(e_s(a))_{s\in S}\ &=(e_s(\varphi(a))_{s\in S}\ &=
u_B(\varphi(a)) \end{align*} holds. It means $(
u_A)_{A\in\mathcal{V}(C)}$ is a natural transformation.
nodes.statement_short: Verify the naturality square.

nodes.name: Set up square
nodes.statement: Let $A,B\in\mathcal{V}(C)$ and $\varphi:A\rightarrow B$ be a homomorphism. We should the diagram \[\xymatrix{ A\ar[r]^{\nu_A} \ar[d]_\varphi& {\rm H}(A_d)\ar[d]^{{\rm H}(\varphi_d)}\\ B\ar[r]^{\nu_B} & {\rm H}(B_d) }\] commute.
nodes.statement_short: Fix a homomorphism and the square to check.

nodes.name: Compute
nodes.statement: For $a\in A$, \begin{align*} {\rm H}(\varphi_d)(\nu_A(a)) &={\rm H}(\varphi_d)(e_s(a))_{s\in S}\\ &=(\varphi(e_s(a))_{s\in S}\\ &=(e_s(\varphi(a))_{s\in S}\\ &=\nu_B(\varphi(a)) \end{align*} holds.
nodes.statement_short: Chase an element around the square.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: It means $(\nu_A)_{A\in\mathcal{V}(C)}$ is a natural transformation.
nodes.statement_short: Naturality holds.

nodes.name: Diagonal pair of ${\rm H}(M)$
nodes.statement: First, we prove $(d,(e_s)_{s\in S})$ is a diagonal pair of ${\rm H}(M)$. 1. $e_s\circ d=e_s\circ \pi_{(S,s)}$ is proved as follows: \[ e_sd = e_s(\pi_{(S\times S,p_2,(t,t))}^M)_{t\in S} =e_s(\pi_{(S\times S,p_2,(s,t))}^M)_{t\in S} = e_s\circ \pi_{(S,s)}^{{\rm H}(M)}. \] Here and through the proof of this proposition, $\pi^M$ and $\pi^{{\rm H}(M)}$ denote projection constants of $M$ and ${\rm H}(M)$ respectively. 2. $d\circ(e_s\circ\pi_{(S,s)})=d$ is proved as follows: \begin{align*} d(e_s\circ \pi_{(S,s)}^{{\rm H}(M)})_{s\in S} &= (\pi_{(S\times S,p_2,(s,s))})_{s\in S} \circ (e_{s,t}\pi_{(S,\mathrm{id},s)}^M\circ (\pi_{(S\times S,p_2,(s,u))})_{u\in S})_{(s,t)\in S\times S}\\ &=(e_{s,s}\pi_{(S,\mathrm{id},s)}^M\circ (\pi_{(S\times S,p_2,(s,u))}^M)_{u\in S})_{s\in S} \\ &=(\pi_{(S\times S,p_2,(s,s))}^M)_{s\in S}\\ &=d. \end{align*} 3. $d\circ(\pi_{(S,0)})_{s\in S}=\pi_{(S,0)}$ is proved as follows: \begin{align*} d\circ (\pi_{(S,0)}^{{\rm H}(M)})_{s\in S} &=(\pi_{(S\times S,p_2,(s,s))}^M)_{s\in S} \circ (\pi_{(S\times S,p_2,(0,t))}^M)_{(s,t)\in S\times S}\\ &=(\pi_{(S\times S,p_2,(0,s))}^M)_{s\in S}\\ &=\pi_{(S,0)}^{{\rm H}(M)}. \end{align*} We complete the proof that $(d,(e_s)_{s\in S})$ is a diagonal pair of ${\rm H}(M)$.
nodes.statement_short: Verify the three diagonal-pair identities in ${\rm H}(M)$.

nodes.statement: 1. $e_s\circ d=e_s\circ \pi_{(S,s)}$ is proved as follows: \[ e_sd = e_s(\pi_{(S\times S,p_2,(t,t))}^M)_{t\in S} =e_s(\pi_{(S\times S,p_2,(s,t))}^M)_{t\in S} = e_s\circ \pi_{(S,s)}^{{\rm H}(M)}. \] Here and through the proof of this proposition, $\pi^M$ and $\pi^{{\rm H}(M)}$ denote projection constants of $M$ and ${\rm H}(M)$ respectively.
nodes.statement_short: Identity $e_s\circ d=e_s\circ\pi_{(S,s)}$.

nodes.statement: 2. $d\circ(e_s\circ\pi_{(S,s)})=d$ is proved as follows: \begin{align*} d(e_s\circ \pi_{(S,s)}^{{\rm H}(M)})_{s\in S} &= (\pi_{(S\times S,p_2,(s,s))})_{s\in S} \circ (e_{s,t}\pi_{(S,\mathrm{id},s)}^M\circ (\pi_{(S\times S,p_2,(s,u))})_{u\in S})_{(s,t)\in S\times S}\\ &=(e_{s,s}\pi_{(S,\mathrm{id},s)}^M\circ (\pi_{(S\times S,p_2,(s,u))}^M)_{u\in S})_{s\in S} \\ &=(\pi_{(S\times S,p_2,(s,s))}^M)_{s\in S}\\ &=d. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Identity $d\circ(e_s\pi_{(S,s)})=d$.

nodes.statement: 3. $d\circ(\pi_{(S,0)})_{s\in S}=\pi_{(S,0)}$ is proved as follows: \begin{align*} d\circ (\pi_{(S,0)}^{{\rm H}(M)})_{s\in S} &=(\pi_{(S\times S,p_2,(s,s))}^M)_{s\in S} \circ (\pi_{(S\times S,p_2,(0,t))}^M)_{(s,t)\in S\times S}\\ &=(\pi_{(S\times S,p_2,(0,s))}^M)_{s\in S}\\ &=\pi_{(S,0)}^{{\rm H}(M)}. \end{align*} We complete the proof that $(d,(e_s)_{s\in S})$ is a diagonal pair of ${\rm H}(M)$.
nodes.statement_short: Identity $d\circ(\pi_{(S,0)})=\pi_{(S,0)}$; diagonal pair established.

nodes.name: (Injectivity of $\mu$)
nodes.statement: (Injectivity of $\mu_{(\lambda,v,s)}$) Let $f,g\in M_{(\lambda,v,s)}$ and assume $\mu_{(\lambda,v,s)}(f)=\mu_{(\lambda,v,s)}(g)$, namely, \begin{align*} &e_{s,t}f\circ(\pi_{(\lambda\times S,p_2,(i,v(i))}^M))_{i\in\lambda} \circ (e_{v(i),u}\pi_{(\lambda\times S,p_2,(i,v(i))})_{(i,u)\in\lambda\times S}\\ =&e_{s,t}g\circ(\pi_{(\lambda\times S,p_2,(i,v(i))}^M))_{i\in\lambda} \circ (e_{v(i),u}\pi_{(\lambda\times S,p_2,(i,v(i))})_{(i,u)\in\lambda\times S} \end{align*} hold for all $t\in S$. Notice that the following two equations hold: The first equation is \begin{align*} &\pi_{(\lambda,v,v(i))}^M\\ =&e_{v(i),v(i)}\circ \pi_{(\lambda,v,v(i))}^M \\ =&\pi_{(\lambda\times S,p_2,(i,v(i)))}^M \circ (e_{v(j),u}\circ \pi_{(\lambda,v,v(j))}^M)_{(j,u)\in\lambda\times S} \end{align*} The second equation is \[ \mathrm{id}_s:=\pi_{(\{s\},\mathrm{id}_{\{s\}},s)}^M=e_{s,s}\pi_{(S,\mathrm{id}_S,s)}^M (e_{s,t})_{t\in S}. \] By these equations injectivity of $\mu_{(\lambda,v,s)}$ is proved as follows: \begin{align*} f &=\mathrm{id}_s\circ f\circ (\pi_{(\lambda,v,v(i))}^M)_{i\in\lambda}\\ &=e_{s,s}\pi_{(S,\mathrm{id},s)}^M (e_{s,t})_{t\in S}\circ f (\pi_{(\lambda\times S,p_2,(i,v(i)))}^M)_{i\in\lambda} \circ (e_{v(j),u}\circ \pi_{(\lambda,v,v(j))}^M)_{(j,u)\in \lambda\times S}\\ &=e_{s,s}\pi_{(S,\mathrm{id},s)}^M (e_{s,t})_{t\in S}\circ g (\pi_{(\lambda\times S,p_2,(i,v(i)))}^M)_{i\in\lambda} \circ (e_{v(j),u}\circ \pi_{(\lambda,v,v(j))}^M)_{(j,u)\in \lambda\times S}\\ &=g. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Two auxiliary identities let $f$ be recovered from $\mu(f)$.

nodes.name: (Surjectivity of $\mu$)
nodes.statement: (Surjectivity of $\mu_{(\lambda,v,s)}$) Let $f/\mathclose\sim\in ({\rm H}(M))_{d,(\lambda,v,s)}$. Define $\tilde{f}$ by $\tilde{f}=\pi_{(S,\mathrm{id},s)}^M\circ f\circ (e_{v(i),u}\circ\pi_{(\lambda,v,i)})_{(i,u)\in \lambda\times S}$. Then the following formula holds. \begin{align*} \mu_{(\lambda,v,s)}(\tilde{f}) &=\left((e_{s,t})_{t\in S}\circ \tilde{f}\circ ( \pi_{(\lambda\times S,p_2,(i,v(i)))}^M)_{i\in\lambda}\right)/\mathclose\sim\\ &=\left((e_{s,t})_{t\in S}\circ \pi_{(S,\mathrm{id},s)}^M\circ f\circ (e_{v(i),u}\circ \pi_{(\lambda,v,i)}^M)_{(i,u)\in \lambda\times S}\circ (\pi_{(\lambda\times S,p_2,(i,v(i)))}^M)_{i\in\lambda}\right)/\mathclose\sim\\ &=\left(e_s\circ f\circ (e_{v(i),u}\circ \pi_{(\lambda,v,i)}^M)_{(i,u)\in \lambda\times S}\circ (\pi_{(\lambda\times S,p_2,(i,v(i)))}^M)_{i\in\lambda}\right)/\mathclose\sim\\ &=\left(f\circ (e_{v(i),u}\circ \pi_{(\lambda\times S,p_2,(i,v(i)))}^M)_{(i,u)\in\lambda\times S}\right)/\mathclose\sim\\ &= f/\mathclose\sim. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Explicit preimage $\tilde f$.

nodes.name: (Compatibility of $\mu$)
nodes.statement: (Compatibility of $\mu$) Let $f\in M_{(\lambda_1,v_1,s)}$ and $g_i\in M_{(\lambda_2,v_2,v_1(i))}$ for $i\in\lambda_1$. Then \begin{align*} &\mu_{(\lambda_2,v_2,s)}(f\circ (g_i)_{i\in\lambda_1})\\ =&\left((e_{s,t})_{t\in S}\circ f\circ (g_i)_{i\in\lambda_1} \circ (\pi_{(\lambda_2\times S,p_2,(j,v_2(j))}^M)_{j\in\lambda_2}\right)/\mathclose\sim\\ =&\left((e_{s,t})_{t\in S}\circ f\circ (e_{v_1(i),v_1(i)}g_i)_{i\in\lambda_1} \circ (\pi_{(\lambda_2\times S,p_2,(j,v_2(j))}^M)_{j\in\lambda_2}\right)/\mathclose\sim\\ =&\left((e_{s,t})_{t\in S}\circ f \circ (\pi_{(\lambda_1\times S,p_2,(i,v_1(i))}^M)_{i\in\lambda_1} \circ (e_{v_1(i),u})_{(i,u)\in\lambda_1\times S}\circ (g_i)_{i\in\lambda_1} \circ (\pi_{(\lambda_2\times S,p_2,(j,v_2(j))}^M)_{j\in\lambda_2}\right)/\mathclose\sim\\ =&\mu_{(\lambda_1,v_1,s)}(f)\circ (\mu_{(\lambda_2,v_2,v_1(i))}(g_i))_{i\in\lambda_1}. \end{align*} We complete the proof of the proposition.
nodes.statement_short: $\mu$ preserves composition.

nodes.name: Homomorphism
nodes.statement: Let $f\in M_{(\lambda,v,s)}$ and $a_i\in A_{v(i)}$ for $i\in\lambda$. Then \begin{align*} \mu_{(\lambda,v,s)}(f)(\mu_{A,v(i)}(a_i))_{i\in\lambda} &=(e_{s,t})_{t\in S}\circ f\circ (\pi_{(\lambda\times S,p_2,(i,v(i)))})_{i\in\lambda} (e_{v(i),u}(a_i))_{(i,u)\in\lambda\times S}\\ &=(e_{s,t})_{t\in S}\circ f(e_{v(i),v(i)}(a_i))_{i\in\lambda}\\ &=(e_{s,t})_{t\in S}\circ f(a_i)_{i\in\lambda}\\ &=\mu_{A,s}(f(a_i)_{i\in\lambda}). \end{align*} This equation is nothing but the proposition stated.
nodes.statement_short: Compute that $\mu_A$ commutes with term actions.

nodes.name: Naturality
nodes.statement: We prove $(\mu_A)_{A\in\mathcal{V}(M)}$ is a natural transformation. Let $A=(A_s)_{s\in S},B=(B_s)_{s\in S}\in \mathcal{V}(M)$ and $\varphi=(\varphi_s)_{s\in S}$ be a homomorphism $A\rightarrow B$. We prove should the diagram \[\xymatrix{ A\ar[r]^{\mu_A} \ar[d]_\varphi& ({\rm H}(A))_d\ar[d]^{({\rm H}(\varphi))_d}\\ B\ar[r]^{\mu_B} & ({\rm H}(B))_d }\] commute. For $s\in S$ and $a\in A_s$, the equation \begin{align*} \mu_{B,s}(\varphi_s(a)) &=(e_{s,t}(\varphi_s(a))_{t\in S}\\ &=(\varphi_t(e_{s,t}(a)))_{t\in S}\\ &={\rm H}(\varphi)(e_{s,t}(a))_{t\in S}\\ &=({\rm H}(\varphi))_{d,s}(\mu_{A,s}(a)) \end{align*} holds. This is nothing but $\mu_B\circ \varphi=({\rm H}(\varphi))_d\circ \mu_A$, thus it is proved that $(\mu_A)_{A\in\mathcal{V}(M)}$ is a natural transformation.
nodes.statement_short: Verify the naturality square.

nodes.name: Reduction
nodes.statement: We only show that any subalgebra of ${\rm H}(A)$ is in the form ${\rm H}(B)$ by a subalgebra $B$ of $A$. Other parts are easily verified or proved similarly. If ${\rm H}(A)= \emptyset$, then the assertion is trivial. Thus, we assume $A_s\neq\emptyset$ for all $s\in S$.
nodes.statement_short: Only the subalgebra correspondence is proved, and only for non-empty sorts.

nodes.name: Define $B_s$
nodes.statement: Let $B'$ be a subalgebra of ${\rm H}(A)$. Define \[ B_s:=\{b\in A_s\mid\exists (a_t)_{t\in S\setminus\{s\}}\in\prod_{t\in S\setminus\{s\}}A_t; (b,(a_t)_{t\in S\setminus\{s\}})\in B'\}. \] Clearly, $B'\subset \prod_{s\in S}B_s$ holds.
nodes.statement_short: Project $B'$ to each sort to define $B_s$; clearly $B'\subset\prod B_s$.

nodes.name: Reverse inclusion via diagonal term
nodes.statement: We show $\prod_{s\in S}B_s\subset B'$. Let $(b_s)_{s\in S}\in \prod_{s\in S}B_s$. By definition of $B_s$, there exist $(c_{st})_{t\in S}\in B'$ such that $c_{ss}=b_s$. Let $d=(\pi_{(S\times S,p_2,(s,s))})_{s\in S}$ be the diagonal term. Then \[ B'\ni d((c_{st})_{t\in s})_{s\in S}=(c_{ss})_{s\in S}=(b_s)_{s\in s}. \qedhere \]
nodes.statement_short: Apply the diagonal term to elements of $B'$ to get $\prod B_s\subset B'$.

nodes.name: Chain of equalities
nodes.statement: We show \begin{equation} {\rm H}(\mathcal{V}(\mathcal{K}))=\mathcal{V}({\rm H}(\mathcal{K}))=\mathbf{HSP}({\rm H}(\mathcal{K}))={\rm H}(\mathbf{HSP}(\mathcal{K})). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: State the chain of equalities to be shown.

nodes.name: Second and last equalities
nodes.statement: The second equality is Birkhoff's variety theorem for classes of single-sorted algebras. The last equality follows from Proposition \ref{sub-con-corresopndence}.
nodes.statement_short: Birkhoff's theorem and Proposition 7.2 give the second and last equalities.

nodes.name: First equality
nodes.statement: The first equality is proved as follows. For $f,g\in {\rm H}_\lambda(M)$, where $f=(f_s)_{s\in S}$, $g=(g_s)_{s\in S}$, the following equivalence holds: \begin{align*} {\rm H}(\mathcal{V}(\mathcal{K}))\models f=g \Longleftrightarrow& \forall s\in S;\ \mathcal{V}(\mathcal{K})\models f_s=g_s\\ \Longleftrightarrow& \forall s\in S;\ \mathcal{K}\models f_s=g_s\\ \Longleftrightarrow& {\rm H}(\mathcal{K})\models f=g\\ \Longleftrightarrow& \mathcal{V}({\rm H}(\mathcal{K}))\models f=g. \end{align*} It means the equational theories defining $\mathcal{V}({\rm H}(\mathcal{K}))$ and ${\rm H}(\mathcal{V}(\mathcal{K}))$ coincide with each other. Therefore, ${\rm H}(\mathcal{V}(\mathcal{K}))=\mathcal{V}({\rm H}(\mathcal{K}))$ holds.
nodes.statement_short: Equational theories of ${\rm H}(\mathcal{V}(\mathcal{K}))$ and $\mathcal{V}({\rm H}(\mathcal{K}))$ coincide.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: By (\ref{varieties-through-homogenization}) and Theorem \ref{main-theorem-categorical-equivalence}, $\mathcal{V}(\mathcal{K})=\mathbf{HSP}(\mathcal{K})$ holds.
nodes.statement_short: Combine with the categorical equivalence to conclude.

nodes.name: 1 iff 2
nodes.statement: 1 $\Leftrightarrow$ 2 is an easy consequence of Proposition \ref{sub-con-corresopndence}.
nodes.statement_short: Transfer via Proposition 7.2.

nodes.name: 2 iff 3 iff 4, 5 implies 4
nodes.statement: 2 $\Leftrightarrow$ 3 is well known Mal'cev's theorem (See e.g.{\cite[Theorem 12.2]{BS}}). 3 $\Leftrightarrow$ 4 follows from the definition of homogenization. 5 $\Rightarrow$ 4 is trivial.
nodes.statement_short: Classical Mal'cev theorem; $3\Leftrightarrow4$ by definition of homogenization; $5\Rightarrow4$ trivial.

nodes.name: 1 implies 5
nodes.statement: 1 $\Rightarrow$ 5. Let $F$ be a rank $(3\delta_{st})_{t\in S}$ free algebra, namely, there are three elements $a,b,c$ of sort $s$ such that $\{a,b,c\}$ freely generates $F$. Let $\theta$ and $\eta$ be congruences of $F$ generated by $(a,b)$ and $(b,c)$ respectively. Then $(a,c)\in\theta\circ\eta=\eta\circ\theta$, namely, there is $x\in F_s$ such that $(a,x)\in \eta$, $(x,c)\in\theta$. Let $p_s$ be the term corresponding to $x$, then equations stated in Condition 5 hold.
nodes.statement_short: Free algebra on three generators of sort $s$ yields sortwise Mal'cev terms.

nodes.name: Condition 1
nodes.statement: Condition 1 of this corollary is equivalent to that $\mathcal{V}_d$ satisfy the condition 1 of the previous theorem.
nodes.statement_short: Condition 1 matches condition 1 of Theorem 7.14.

nodes.name: Condition 2
nodes.statement: Condition 2 of this corollary is equivalent to that $\mathcal{V}_d$ satisfy the condition 5 of the previous theorem.
nodes.statement_short: Condition 2 matches condition 5 of Theorem 7.14.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Thus, these conditions are equivalent.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude equivalence.

nodes.name: Analogy with Mal'cev
nodes.statement: Equivalence of 1,2,3 and 4 is similar to corresponding equivalence of Theorem \ref{malcev}.
nodes.statement_short: 1-4 as in Theorem 7.14.

nodes.name: Jónsson and easy implications
nodes.statement: 2 $\Leftrightarrow$ 3 is known as J\'onsson's theorem (See e.g. {\cite[Theorem 12.6]{BS}}). 5 $\Rightarrow$ 4 easily follows from finiteness of $S$. 6 $\Rightarrow$ 5 is trivial.
nodes.statement_short: Jónsson's theorem; $5\Rightarrow4$ by finiteness of $S$; $6\Rightarrow5$ trivial.

nodes.name: 1 implies 6
nodes.statement: 1 $\Rightarrow$ 6. Let $F$ be a rank $(3\delta_{st})_{t\in S}$ free algebra of $\mathcal{V}(M)$, $\{a,b,c\}$ be a set of free generators of $F$, and $\theta,\eta,\zeta$ be the congruences of $F$ generated by $(a,c),(a,b),(b,c)$ respectively. Then \[ (a,c)\in \theta\land(\eta\lor\zeta)=(\theta\land\eta)\lor(\theta\land\zeta). \] By finiteness of arity of $M$, the join in congruence lattice is described as $\alpha\lor\beta=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb{N}}(\alpha\circ\beta)^n$, where $(\alpha\circ\beta)^n$ denotes the $k$-th relational power of $\alpha\circ\beta$. Thus, there are $x_0,\dots,x_{2n}$ such that \[ x_0=a,x_{2n}=c,(x_{2i},x_{2i+1})\in\theta\land\eta, (x_{2i-1},x_{2i})\in\theta\land\zeta. \] The terms $d_{s,i}$ corresponding to $x_i$ satisfy the equations stated in Condition 6.
nodes.statement_short: Free-algebra argument with finitary joins of congruences.

nodes.statement: 1. Each $C_n$ has J\'onsson term, thus $\mathcal{V}(C_n)$ is congruence distributive. Thus, \[ \mathcal{V}(C)=\mathcal{V}\left(\prod_{n\in\mathbb{N}}C_n\right){\simeq} \bigotimes_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\mathcal{V}(C_n) \] is congruence distributive. Here, $\otimes_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\mathcal{V}(C_n)$ denotes non-indexed product of the family $\{\mathcal{V}(C_n)\}_{n\in \mathbb{N}}$ of varieties. By Proposition \ref{sub-con-corresopndence}, $\mathcal{V}(C_d)$ also be congruence distributive.
nodes.statement_short: Congruence distributivity from the factors and Proposition 7.2.

nodes.statement: 2. If $C$ has J\'onsson term of length $n$, then $C_{n+1}$ also has J\'onsson term of length $n$. It is verified by the induction on $n$ that this is impossible.
nodes.statement_short: No Jónsson term, by induction on $n$.

nodes.statement: 3. It is easily verified that $e_n(C)$ is isomorphic to $C_n$. Particularly, $e_n(C)$ has J\'onsson term. These are nothing but the terms of $C_d$ satisfying Condition 6 of the theorem.
nodes.statement_short: $e_n(C)\cong C_n$ has a Jónsson term.

nodes.statement: 4. Let $f\in C_{d,(\aleph_0,v,n)}$, where $v:\aleph_0\rightarrow \mathbb{N}$ and $n\in\mathbb{N}$. By the definition of heterogenization, $f$ is represented by $\tilde{f}\in C_{\aleph_0}$ such that $e_n\circ\tilde{f}=\tilde{f}$. This condition implies that the $n$-th component of $\tilde{f}$ is an element of $C_n$ (it is finitary), and other components are $u$ (depend no variables). Therefore, $\tilde{f}$, particularly $f$, is finitary.
nodes.statement_short: Representatives are finitary, so $C_d$ is essentially finitary.
